name: Horsehead Nebula
description: The Horsehead Nebula is a small dark nebula located about 1,375 light-years from Earth in the constellation of Orion. The nebula is located just to the south of Alnitak, the easternmost star of Orion's Belt, and is part of the much larger Orion molecular cloud complex.

name: IC 10
description: IC 10 is an irregular galaxy in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was discovered by American astronomer Lewis Swift on 8 October 1887.

name: Sadr Region
description: IC 1318 is the diffuse emission nebula and a H II region surrounding the star Sadr at the center of Cygnus's cross thus getting a nickname Sadr Region. The Sadr Region is one of the surrounding nebulous regions; others include the Butterfly Nebula and the Crescent Nebula.

name: Elephant Trunk Nebula
description: IC 1396 is a large emission nebulae, a region of ionized gas, located in the constellation Cepheus about 2,400 light years away from Earth.

name: Fish Head Nebula
description: IC 1795 is a bright emission nebula in Cassiopeia, the glowing knot of gas and dust at the northwest edge of the larger Heart Nebula (IC 1805). Its ridges of ionized hydrogen and dark dust lanes take on the shape of a fish's head in wide-field images, which is how it got its common name. It lies in the Perseus arm of the Milky Way, part of the same star-forming complex as the Heart and Soul nebulae, roughly 7,500 light-years away.

name: Heart Nebula
description: The Heart Nebula is an emission nebula, 7,500 light-years (2,300 pc) away from Earth and located in the Perseus Arm of the Galaxy in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was discovered by William Herschel on 3 November 1787.

name: Soul Nebula
description: Westerhout 5 is an emission nebula located in Cassiopeia. Several small open clusters are embedded in the nebula: Collinder 33 and 34 in the head and IC 1848 in the body.

name: Witch Head Nebula
description: The Witch Head Nebula is a large, faint reflection nebula in Eridanus about 900 light-years away, its elongated shape evoking the profile of a cackling witch. Illuminated by Rigel, the blue supergiant in Orion just to its east, its colour comes from preferential blue-wavelength scattering off fine interstellar dust. It is one of the most challenging objects to observe visually but yields a haunting result in deep photographs.

name: Seagull Nebula
description: IC 2177 is a region of nebulosity that lies along the border between the constellations Monoceros and Canis Major. It is a roughly circular H II region centered on the Be star HD 53367.

name: Hidden Galaxy
description: IC 342 is a large, face-on spiral galaxy in Camelopardalis about 10.7 million light-years away, among the brightest spirals in the sky if not for obscuring dust and stars of the Milky Way that dim it by roughly 2 magnitudes. It is the dominant member of the IC 342/Maffei Group, one of the closest galaxy groups to our Local Group. Its extensive spiral arms and active central starburst ring are well resolved in long-exposure photographs even through the heavy foreground absorption.

name: Flaming Star Nebula
description: The Flaming Star Nebula (IC 405) is an emission and reflection nebula in Auriga about 1,500 light-years away, energized and illuminated by the hot runaway O-type star AE Aurigae, which is not gravitationally bound to the nebula but simply passing through it. The distinctive reddish emission from hydrogen and blue reflected starlight give the nebula a two-tone flame-like appearance in color photographs. AE Aurigae was likely ejected from the Orion Nebula region millions of years ago in a close encounter between two binary stars.

name: Tadpoles Nebula
description: IC 410 is an emission nebula in the constellation of Auriga. It is part of a larger star-forming complex that includes the nearby IC 405 and the open clusters M36 and M38.

name: Spider Nebula
description: IC 417 is an emission nebula in Auriga. It is part of the Aur OB2 association, located nearby to NGC 1931. It is located on the near side of the Perseus Arm of the Milky Way galaxy.

name: Horsehead Nebula
description: IC 434 is a bright emission nebula in the equatorial constellation of Orion. It was discovered on February 1, 1786, by German-British astronomer William Herschel.

name: Jellyfish Nebula
description: IC 443 is a galactic supernova remnant (SNR) in the constellation Gemini. On the plane of the sky, it is located near the star Eta Geminorum. Its distance is roughly 5,000 light years from Earth.

name: Prawn Nebula
description: Prawn Nebula, also known as IC 4628, is an emission nebula located in the Sagittarius Arm of the Milky Way, around 6,000 light-years from Earth in the constellation Scorpius. It forms part of the tail of the "False Comet" anchored by the bright open cluster NGC 6231.

name: IC 4756
description: IC 4756 is a large bright open cluster in the constellation Serpens. Known as Graff's Cluster, it is bright enough to be seen with the naked eye and considered a fine cluster for binoculars or small telescopes.

name: Pelican Nebula
description: The Pelican Nebula is an H II region associated with the North America Nebula in the constellation of Cygnus. The gaseous contortions of this emission nebula bear a resemblance to a pelican, giving rise to its name.

name: Cocoon Nebula
description: The Cocoon Nebula (IC 5146) is an emission and reflection nebula in Cygnus about 4,000 light-years away, surrounding the young open cluster Collinder 470 at its centre. A long dark nebula catalogued as Barnard 168 stretches westward from the Cocoon, a dense molecular filament from which the cluster and nebula are still actively forming. Long-exposure narrowband images reveal a richly structured interior of hot gas and embedded young stars wrapped in the cocoon of surrounding dust.

name: Crab Nebula
description: The Crab Nebula is the remnant of a supernova explosion observed by Chinese and Arab astronomers in July 1054 CE. Located about 6,500 light-years away in Taurus, its tangled filaments of glowing gas span roughly 11 light-years and continue expanding at 1,500 km per second. A rapidly spinning neutron star called the Crab Pulsar sits at the core, powering the nebula's intense X-ray and optical emission.

name: Messier 10
description: Messier 10 is a bright globular cluster about 14,300 light-years away in Ophiuchus, spanning roughly 83 light-years across. Its moderately loose central concentration makes individual stars relatively easy to resolve in medium-aperture telescopes. Its apparent neighbor M12 lies just three degrees away in the same field of view.

name: Messier 100
description: Messier 100 is one of the largest and brightest spirals in the Virgo Cluster, about 55 million light-years away in Coma Berenices, and a showcase example of a grand design spiral with two well-defined main arms. Hubble Space Telescope Cepheid observations in this galaxy in 1994 provided a key early measurement of the Hubble Constant. Several supernovae have been discovered in its disk, and its multiple tightly wound arms are magnificent in photographs.

name: Pinwheel Galaxy
description: The Pinwheel Galaxy is a large, nearly face-on spiral galaxy about 20.9 million light-years away in Ursa Major, spanning roughly 170,000 light-years, nearly twice the diameter of the Milky Way. Its vast, asymmetric spiral arms are dotted with giant HII regions and luminous blue star clusters, and the galaxy interacts gravitationally with several smaller companions that distort its arms. The Type II supernova SN 2023ixf, discovered in 2023, was one of the nearest supernovae in recent decades.

name: Spindle Galaxy
description: The Spindle Galaxy is a lenticular galaxy in Draco about 44.9 million light-years away, seen nearly edge-on with a dark equatorial dust lane cutting through a prominent lens-shaped bulge. Its identity as Messier 102 was debated for nearly two centuries, with some arguing Messier intended to list NGC 5866 while others claimed it was a duplicate observation of M101. The dark lane and smooth stellar disk make it one of the more striking lenticular galaxies in moderate-aperture telescopes.

name: Messier 103
description: Messier 103 is an open cluster of about 40 stars in Cassiopeia, approximately 8,500 light-years away. Several red and blue giant stars provide an attractive color contrast visible in small telescopes. It was the last object added to the Messier catalog by Messier himself, with subsequent entries added posthumously by other astronomers.

name: Sombrero Galaxy
description: The Sombrero Galaxy is one of the most visually striking galaxies in the sky, viewed nearly edge-on with a prominent dark dust lane slicing through a brilliant white core. Lying about 31.1 million light-years away in Virgo, it has an unusually massive central bulge and harbors a black hole of roughly one billion solar masses at its nucleus. Its rich system of about 2,000 globular clusters and exceptional central brightness make it a favorite for both amateur observers and professional astronomers.

name: Messier 105
description: Messier 105 is the brightest elliptical galaxy in the Leo I Group, about 32 million light-years away in Leo. Unlike most ellipticals, it shows evidence of relatively recent low-level star formation in its core and harbors a supermassive central black hole of roughly 200 million solar masses. It is usually photographed alongside its companions NGC 3371 and NGC 3373 in a compact group.

name: Messier 106
description: Messier 106 is a Seyfert 2 spiral galaxy in Canes Venatici about 23.7 million light-years away, famous for being one of a handful of galaxies with precisely measured distances using water maser emission from its active nucleus. The maser traces a nearly edge-on disk of gas orbiting a 36-million-solar-mass central black hole, allowing a geometric distance measurement independent of the cosmic distance ladder. Strikingly, it has two anomalous arms of hot, jet-driven gas spiraling outward from the nucleus visible in radio and X-ray images alongside two normal optical spiral arms.

name: Messier 107
description: Messier 107 is a loosely concentrated globular cluster in Ophiuchus about 20,900 light-years from Earth, one of the least concentrated Messier globulars. It contains several dark patches believed to be dust lanes within the cluster, an unusual feature for globulars. It spans roughly 80 light-years in diameter and was one of the last objects admitted to the Messier catalog, added in 1947.

name: Surfboard Galaxy
description: The Surfboard Galaxy is a barred spiral in Ursa Major seen nearly edge-on, about 45 million light-years away. Its ragged, mottled profile lacks a prominent central bulge, giving it a rough cigar shape broken by dark dust lanes and scattered bright HII regions. It lies just 48 arcminutes from the Owl Nebula (M97), and both are a dramatic pairing in a wide-field photograph.

name: Messier 109
description: Messier 109 is a barred spiral galaxy in Ursa Major about 67.1 million light-years away, the most distant of the Messier galaxies assigned a specific identity. Its striking bar structure connects a bright nucleus to two main spiral arms, making it an excellent example of an SBb-type galaxy. Three dwarf satellite galaxies orbit it in a compact group.

name: Wild Duck Cluster
description: The Wild Duck Cluster is one of the richest and most compact open clusters known, packing around 2,900 stars into a region only 21 light-years across some 6,200 light-years away in Scutum. The dense fan shape of its brightest stars recalls a flight of wild ducks in motion. Its estimated age of 250 million years places it among the older open clusters still holding together.

name: Messier 110
description: Messier 110 is the second-largest satellite galaxy of the Andromeda Galaxy, a dwarf elliptical about 2.69 million light-years away. Unusually for a galaxy of its type, it contains patches of dark dust and evidence of relatively recent star formation, suggesting a more complex history than typical dwarf ellipticals. Its faint, elongated glow is visible alongside M31 and M32 in binoculars under dark skies.

name: Messier 12
description: Messier 12 is a loosely concentrated globular cluster in Ophiuchus, about 15,700 light-years away and spanning roughly 75 light-years. Compared with the denser M10 nearby, it appears more open and is easier to resolve into stars with smaller instruments. Studies suggest it has lost a substantial fraction of its low-mass stars through tidal stripping by the Milky Way over billions of years.

name: Hercules Cluster
description: The Great Hercules Cluster is one of the finest globular clusters in the northern sky, containing around 300,000 stars in a sphere about 145 light-years across at a distance of 22,200 light-years. Estimated to be roughly 11.65 billion years old, it is a resolved, glittering ball of stars in almost any telescope. In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope broadcast a message in its direction, though at 22,000 light-years the reply is some way off.

name: Messier 14
description: Messier 14 is a moderately concentrated globular cluster about 30,300 light-years away in Ophiuchus, containing roughly 150,000 stars across about 100 light-years. A nova was observed within it in 1938, though it went unnoticed until old photographic plates were examined in 1964. Its greater distance compared to nearby Ophiuchus clusters gives it a relatively faint, unresolved appearance in small telescopes.

name: Messier 15
description: The Great Pegasus Cluster is one of the most densely packed globular clusters known, its core having undergone gravitational collapse to create an extraordinary central stellar density. Sitting 33,600 light-years away in Pegasus, it contains over 100,000 stars and is home to the planetary nebula Pease 1, one of only four known planetary nebulae inside a globular cluster. It is also one of the most metal-poor clusters, composed largely of stars from the very early universe.

name: Eagle Nebula
description: The Eagle Nebula is a young open cluster embedded in an active emission nebula in Serpens, roughly 5,700 light-years from Earth. It became globally famous in 1995 when the Hubble Space Telescope revealed the Pillars of Creation, towering columns of gas and dust where new stars are forming at this moment. The cluster itself contains dozens of hot O-type and B-type stars whose radiation is slowly eroding and illuminating the surrounding cloud.

name: Omega Nebula
description: The Omega Nebula, also called the Swan Nebula or Horseshoe Nebula, is one of the largest and most active star-forming regions in the Milky Way, located about 5,500 light-years away in Sagittarius. Its bright bar-shaped core glows from intense ultraviolet radiation produced by around 35 embedded O-type stars, while the full cloud complex contains an estimated 30,000 solar masses of ionised gas. Long photographic exposures reveal dramatic filamentary structure stretching away from the central emission.

name: Messier 18
description: Messier 18 is a sparse open cluster of about 20 resolved stars located approximately 4,900 light-years away in Sagittarius. Its hot blue-white B-type stars are estimated to be around 32 million years old, making it a relatively young cluster. It is one of the less visually striking Messier objects but is worth a look while sweeping through the rich surrounding Milky Way fields.

name: Messier 19
description: Messier 19 is one of the most oblate globular clusters known, noticeably flattened along one axis, likely from tidal stress imposed by its proximity to the Galactic Center. Located about 28,000 light-years away in Ophiuchus, it contains several hundred thousand stars in a sphere roughly 140 light-years across. Its estimated age is around 11.9 billion years.

name: Messier 2
description: Messier 2 is one of the largest and richest globular clusters in the Milky Way halo, containing around 150,000 stars packed into a sphere about 175 light-years across. It lies some 37,500 light-years away in Aquarius and is estimated to be around 13 billion years old. Under dark skies it is just visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy star.

name: Trifid Nebula
description: The Trifid Nebula is a striking combination of emission, reflection, and dark nebulae in Sagittarius about 5,200 light-years away. Three dark dust lanes divide the central pink emission region into three lobes, while a blue reflection lobe to the north provides a vivid color contrast. It is one of the most photogenic nebulae in the sky and a popular target for astrophotographers.

name: Messier 21
description: Messier 21 is a young open cluster of around 57 stars in Sagittarius, located about 4,250 light-years from Earth and lying just north of the Trifid Nebula. Dominated by hot blue-white stars, it is estimated to be only about 4.6 million years old. Wide-field views place it alongside the Trifid Nebula and surrounding Milky Way richness for a dramatic combination.

name: Sagittarius Cluster
description: Messier 22 is one of the nearest and brightest globular clusters, only 10,600 light-years away in Sagittarius and spanning about 99 light-years. It is one of four globular clusters known to contain a planetary nebula, and it is bright enough to be visible to the naked eye from dark sites. Its relatively low declination makes it best observed from the southern United States and further south.

name: Messier 23
description: Messier 23 is a rich open cluster of about 150 stars in Sagittarius, lying 2,150 light-years from Earth and spanning roughly 15 light-years. Its membership includes both yellow and orange giant stars alongside hotter blue-white members, giving it a pleasing variety of stellar colors. The cluster's estimated age is around 300 million years.

name: Sagittarius Star Cloud
description: The Sagittarius Star Cloud is not a conventional deep-sky object but a window through the Milky Way's interstellar dust revealing a dense concentration of stars in a distant inner spiral arm. This star cloud spans about 600 by 300 light-years at a distance of roughly 10,000 light-years and appears as the richest concentration of stars visible through binoculars. It is best appreciated at low magnification as a sweeping, glittering field.

name: Messier 25
description: Messier 25 is a scattered open cluster of about 86 stars in Sagittarius, lying about 2,000 light-years away. It is notable for containing U Sagittarii, a bright classical Cepheid variable that pulsates with a period of 6.745 days, serving as a useful distance calibrator. The cluster is estimated to be about 90 million years old.

name: Messier 26
description: Messier 26 is a small open cluster of around 90 stars in Scutum, lying about 5,000 light-years from Earth. Its central region appears less densely populated than its outer parts, possibly due to an obscuring dust cloud. It is relatively faint and requires a telescope to resolve its individual members.

name: Dumbbell Nebula
description: The Dumbbell Nebula was the first planetary nebula ever discovered, found by Charles Messier in 1764, and remains the largest and brightest of its class in the sky. Lying about 1,360 light-years away in Vulpecula, its double-lobed apple-core shape spans 2.5 light-years and glows from ionised hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen energised by the white dwarf at its center. Long exposures reveal a much larger surrounding halo that extends well beyond the bright central region.

name: Messier 28
description: Messier 28 is a compact globular cluster about 18,300 light-years away in Sagittarius, close in the sky to the brighter M22. In 1987 it became the first globular cluster discovered to contain a millisecond pulsar, hinting at a history of stellar collisions and mass transfer in its dense core. It contains roughly 150,000 stars in a sphere about 60 light-years across.

name: Messier 29
description: Messier 29 is a small, sparse open cluster of about 50 stars in Cygnus, embedded in bright Milky Way star fields some 4,000 light-years from Earth. Its five brightest members form a distinctive rectangular box pattern. The cluster is very young at roughly 10 million years old and is partially dimmed by intervening interstellar dust.

name: Messier 3
description: Messier 3 is one of the finest globular clusters in the northern sky, containing roughly 500,000 stars in a sphere about 200 light-years across at a distance of 33,900 light-years. It holds over 270 confirmed RR Lyrae variable stars, more than any other known cluster, making it a benchmark for stellar population studies. Located in Canes Venatici, it is a showpiece target for any telescope.

name: Messier 30
description: Messier 30 is a compact globular cluster in Capricornus, about 28,000 light-years away, whose core has undergone gravitational collapse to produce an extremely high central stellar density. The outer regions show several radial chains of stars extending outward from the nucleus. It contains around 150,000 stars and a substantial population of exotic binary star systems.

name: Andromeda Galaxy
description: The Andromeda Galaxy is the nearest large spiral galaxy to the Milky Way, sitting 2.537 million light-years away in Andromeda and spanning about 220,000 light-years in diameter. Containing roughly one trillion stars, it is the most distant object visible to the naked eye under dark skies. It is on a slow collision course with our galaxy and the two are expected to merge in about 4.5 billion years.

name: Messier 32
description: Messier 32 is a compact dwarf elliptical satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy, about 2.49 million light-years away and visible as a small bright glow just south of M31's core. Despite being tidally distorted by M31, it maintains a remarkably high central surface brightness and hosts an intermediate-mass black hole of roughly 2.5 million solar masses. It is one of the most compact and dense galaxies known.

name: Triangulum Galaxy
description: The Triangulum Galaxy is a spiral galaxy 2.73 million light-years away in Triangulum, the third-largest member of the Local Group after the Milky Way and Andromeda. Its face-on disk spans about 60,000 light-years and contains NGC 604, one of the largest known HII star-forming regions at over 1,500 light-years across. Under excellent dark skies it is just detectable with the naked eye, though its low surface brightness makes it a challenging binocular object.

name: Messier 34
description: Messier 34 is a bright, well-resolved open cluster of about 100 stars in Perseus, lying roughly 1,500 light-years from Earth and spanning 14 light-years. Its members are arranged in long sweeping chains and pairs, dominated by hot blue-white A-type stars. The cluster is estimated to be around 200 million years old.

name: Messier 35
description: Messier 35 is a large, rich open cluster of about 500 stars in Gemini, located approximately 2,800 light-years away. In the same low-power field lies the much more distant cluster NGC 2158, appearing as a hazy background patch 16,000 light-years beyond, creating a striking depth contrast. M35 is around 100 million years old.

name: Pinwheel Cluster
description: Messier 36 is an open cluster of about 60 stars in Auriga, approximately 4,100 light-years away and estimated to be around 25 million years old. It is the smallest and most concentrated of the three Messier clusters in Auriga and is dominated by hot blue-white B-type stars. It has no red giant members, consistent with its young age.

name: Messier 37
description: Messier 37 is the richest and most impressive of the three Messier open clusters in Auriga, containing over 500 stars about 4,500 light-years from Earth. An unusually large number of red giant stars around 12 are scattered among its blue-white members, giving photographs a striking mix of warm and cool colors. Its estimated age of 300 to 550 million years makes it the oldest of the Auriga trio.

name: Starfish Cluster
description: Messier 38 is an open cluster of roughly 100 stars in Auriga about 4,200 light-years away. Its brightest members trace a cross or oblique Greek pi shape. Estimated at around 220 million years old, it sits between the younger M36 and the older M37 in the same Auriga star field.

name: Messier 39
description: Messier 39 is a large, very loose open cluster of about 30 bright stars in Cygnus, lying only 825 light-years from Earth, making it one of the nearest open clusters. It spans roughly 7 light-years and is best viewed at very low magnification due to its wide angular extent. The cluster is around 278 million years old.

name: Messier 4
description: Messier 4 is one of the nearest globular clusters to Earth at only 5,600 light-years in Scorpius. A distinctive bar of stars runs through its core, and it harbors one of the oldest known white dwarf stars, implying an age of 12 to 13 billion years. It is bright enough to resolve individual stars in a small telescope.

name: Winnecke 4
description: Messier 40 (Winnecke 4) is simply a close double star in Ursa Major, not a true nebula or cluster. Messier catalogued it while searching for a nebula reported by the astronomer Hevelius at the same position, finding only this star pair. The two stars lie at different distances and are not physically related.

name: Messier 41
description: Messier 41 is a bright open cluster of about 100 stars in Canis Major, lying 2,300 light-years from Earth just south of Sirius. Several orange giant stars stand out among its blue-white members, providing a warm color contrast visible in binoculars. The cluster spans roughly 25 light-years and is estimated to be 190 to 240 million years old.

name: Orion Nebula
description: The Orion Nebula is the closest large star-forming region to Earth at about 1,344 light-years, and the brightest emission nebula in the sky, faintly visible to the unaided eye as the middle star of Orion's sword. At its heart the Trapezium, a tight cluster of four hot, massive stars, floods the surrounding 24 light-year-wide cloud with ultraviolet radiation. Hubble Space Telescope observations have revealed hundreds of protoplanetary disks and newborn stars still cocooned in gas and dust throughout the nebula.

name: De Mairan's Nebula
description: Messier 43 is a comma-shaped emission nebula separated from the main Orion Nebula by a prominent dark dust lane, at the same distance of about 1,344 light-years. It is ionised by the hot star NU Orionis embedded at its center and forms part of the same vast Orion Molecular Cloud complex as M42. First catalogued by Jean-Jacques Dortous de Mairan in 1731, it is a detached appendage of the greater Orion Nebula system.

name: Beehive Cluster
description: The Beehive Cluster (Praesepe) is one of the nearest open clusters at about 577 light-years in Cancer, containing over 1,000 confirmed members and visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy patch. Two exoplanets have been found orbiting sun-like stars within the cluster, the first planets discovered around main-sequence stars in an open cluster. Its estimated age of around 700 million years makes the Beehive a benchmark for stellar evolution studies.

name: Pleiades
description: The Pleiades are the most recognisable open cluster in the sky, visible to the naked eye as a tight dipper of six or seven stars in Taurus some 444 light-years away. The cluster contains over 1,000 confirmed members, the hottest of which illuminate surrounding interstellar dust in striking electric-blue reflection nebulae visible in photographs. The Pleiades appear in the mythology of cultures worldwide, from ancient Greece to Indigenous Australian traditions spanning tens of thousands of years.

name: Messier 46
description: Messier 46 is a rich open cluster of around 500 stars in Puppis, about 5,400 light-years away. Superimposed near its northern edge is the planetary nebula NGC 2438, a foreground object at only 2,900 light-years that creates the striking illusion of a nebula embedded within the cluster. The cluster's relative faintness at this distance makes it a good binocular or small telescope target in a rich Milky Way field.

name: Messier 47
description: Messier 47 is a bright, coarse open cluster of about 50 stars in Puppis, just 1,600 light-years from Earth. Its brightest members are a mix of blue-white and orange giant stars, visible as colored pinpoints in binoculars. The cluster is roughly 78 million years old and forms a visual pair with M46 just 1.5 degrees to the east.

name: Messier 48
description: Messier 48 is a large, scattered open cluster of about 80 stars in Hydra, 1,500 light-years away. Messier recorded it at incorrect coordinates and the true identity of this object was not confirmed until 1959 when it was matched to NGC 2548. It spans about 23 light-years and has an estimated age of 300 million years.

name: Messier 49
description: Messier 49 is the brightest member of the Virgo Galaxy Cluster and the first galaxy in that cluster to be discovered, located about 56 million light-years away. This giant elliptical contains roughly 6,000 globular clusters, ten times more than the Milky Way, and harbors a supermassive black hole of about 565 million solar masses. It interacts with a smaller companion galaxy and a stream of cold hydrogen gas.

name: Messier 5
description: Messier 5 is an ancient globular cluster in Serpens, estimated to be around 13 billion years old and one of the oldest objects in the Milky Way halo. Lying 24,500 light-years from Earth, it contains several hundred thousand stars spread across 165 light-years. Many observers regard it as the finest northern-hemisphere globular after M13.

name: Messier 50
description: Messier 50 is a rich open cluster of about 200 stars in Monoceros, roughly 3,200 light-years from Earth. A prominent red giant near its center provides a warm color contrast against the surrounding blue-white stars, and the cluster's overall shape is broadly heart-like in photographs. Its estimated age is around 78 million years.

name: Whirlpool Galaxy
description: The Whirlpool Galaxy is a grand design spiral interacting gravitationally with the smaller companion galaxy NGC 5195, about 23 million light-years away in Canes Venatici. William Parsons (Lord Rosse) first recorded its spiral structure in 1845, making it the first galaxy to have that structure recognised. The ongoing interaction has triggered active star formation throughout M51's spiral arms, visible as bright blue star clusters and pink HII regions in photographs.

name: Messier 52
description: Messier 52 is a rich open cluster of about 200 stars in Cassiopeia, embedded in a dense Milky Way field some 5,000 light-years away. Its stars are arranged in a compressed wedge or fan shape, with a luminous orange giant near its southern edge providing a focal point. The cluster's age is estimated at 35 to 135 million years, with some disagreement due to differential reddening.

name: Messier 53
description: Messier 53 is a remote globular cluster in Coma Berenices, about 58,000 light-years away, making it one of the more distant Messier globulars. It spans roughly 220 light-years and contains several hundred thousand stars in a moderately concentrated core. About a degree to the southeast lies the fainter globular NGC 5053, an easy pair for wide-field imaging.

name: Messier 54
description: Messier 54 is a distant globular cluster about 87,000 light-years away in Sagittarius, now understood to be the nucleus or a massive captured cluster of the Sagittarius Dwarf Elliptical Galaxy. The dwarf galaxy is currently being tidally disrupted and absorbed into the Milky Way. M54 contains over one million stars packed into a sphere about 300 light-years across.

name: Messier 55
description: Messier 55 is a large, loosely concentrated globular cluster about 17,600 light-years away in Sagittarius, spanning roughly 100 light-years. Its relatively low stellar density makes individual stars easy to resolve even in a moderate telescope, and it is visually one of the more open-looking Messier globulars. It is best placed for observers in the southern hemisphere.

name: Messier 56
description: Messier 56 is a moderately concentrated globular cluster in Lyra, lying about 32,900 light-years from Earth between the stars Albireo and Sulafat. It contains around 100,000 stars in a sphere roughly 85 light-years across and is estimated to be some 13.7 billion years old. Messier discovered it in 1779 during a comet-hunting session.

name: Ring Nebula
description: The Ring Nebula is one of the most iconic planetary nebulae, appearing as a perfect smoke ring in Lyra about 2,300 light-years away. The glowing shell of ionised gas was expelled by a dying sun-like star several thousand years ago, and the hot white dwarf at the center is visible in images. What appears as a thin ring is actually a cylinder of gas viewed nearly end-on.

name: Messier 58
description: Messier 58 is one of the brightest spiral galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, about 62 million light-years away. One of the few Virgo members with a net blueshift, it is actually approaching our galaxy under the complex gravitational dynamics of the cluster. Its active nucleus hosts a supermassive black hole of around 70 million solar masses.

name: Messier 59
description: Messier 59 is a massive elliptical galaxy in the Virgo Cluster about 60 million light-years away, containing roughly 2,200 globular clusters. Its central black hole is estimated at approximately 270 million solar masses. Though it appears featureless in small telescopes, deep images reveal a complex outer halo hinting at past merger activity.

name: Butterfly Cluster
description: The Butterfly Cluster is a bright open cluster of around 80 stars in Scorpius, located about 1,600 light-years away. Its brightest stars trace a rough butterfly silhouette, dominated by hot blue-white B-type stars plus the luminous orange supergiant BM Scorpii near one wing tip. The cluster is estimated to be about 100 million years old.

name: Messier 60
description: Messier 60 is one of the largest elliptical galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, about 55 million light-years away, interacting with the smaller spiral NGC 4647 to its northwest. Its central black hole is estimated at 4.5 billion solar masses, comparable to the one in M87. Orbiting it is the ultra-compact dwarf galaxy M60-UCD1, itself containing a 21-million-solar-mass black hole.

name: Messier 61
description: Messier 61 is a large face-on barred spiral in the southern Virgo Cluster, about 52.5 million light-years away. It has one of the highest supernova rates of any nearby galaxy, with six recorded supernovae since 1926. Its well-defined bar and multiple spiral arms make it one of the more photogenic Virgo Cluster spirals.

name: Messier 62
description: Messier 62 is an asymmetric globular cluster in Ophiuchus about 22,200 light-years away, its core visibly offset due to tidal forces from the nearby Galactic Center. It is one of the most concentrated globular clusters known and contains at least six millisecond pulsars in its dense interior. Around 150,000 stars inhabit its roughly 100 light-year diameter.

name: Sunflower Galaxy
description: The Sunflower Galaxy is a beautiful flocculent spiral galaxy in Canes Venatici, about 37 million light-years away, whose broken and patchy spiral arms trace a sunflower-like pattern distinct from the grand-design spirals of M51 or M101. It is a member of the M51 Group and contains a bright, compact nucleus surrounded by numerous active star-forming regions scattered through its disk. Its multi-arm structure and smooth texture make it a rewarding target for medium-aperture telescopes.

name: Black Eye Galaxy
description: The Black Eye Galaxy gets its striking name from a dramatic band of dark absorbing dust just in front of its bright nucleus, giving the appearance of a bruised or blackened eye. Located about 24 million light-years away in Coma Berenices, it has a unique inner disk of stars rotating in the opposite direction to the outer disk, thought to be the remnant of a galaxy merger. Long-exposure images reveal a smooth outer elliptical envelope surrounding the turbulent inner disk.

name: Messier 65
description: Messier 65 is an intermediate spiral galaxy about 35 million light-years away in Leo, one of the famous Leo Triplet alongside M66 and NGC 3628. It shows relatively little active star formation and almost no disturbed structure, suggesting it has been less affected by gravitational interactions than its neighbors. Its tightly wound arms and smooth disk make it a photogenic contrast to the ragged NGC 3628.

name: Messier 66
description: Messier 66 is the largest and brightest member of the Leo Triplet, an intermediate spiral about 36 million light-years away in Leo. Gravitational tugs from M65 and NGC 3628 have noticeably distorted its spiral arms and displaced its nucleus from the geometric center of its disk. It shows an elevated rate of star formation in both the nucleus and arms as a result of these interactions.

name: Messier 67
description: Messier 67 is one of the oldest known open clusters, estimated at 3.2 to 5 billion years old, nearly the age of the solar system, making it rare among open clusters that typically disperse within a billion years. Lying about 2,700 light-years away in Cancer, it contains over 500 stars including many sun-like stars with similar age and chemical composition to our own Sun. Its survival is attributed to an orbit that keeps it well above the disruptive star-forming plane of the galaxy.

name: Messier 68
description: Messier 68 is a globular cluster in Hydra about 33,600 light-years from Earth, notable for containing an unusually high number of variable stars, around 250 confirmed members. It spans roughly 106 light-years and appears rich and well-resolved in moderate apertures. Its far southern declination puts it low in the sky for northern observers but well placed from the southern hemisphere.

name: Messier 69
description: Messier 69 is a compact globular cluster in Sagittarius, about 29,700 light-years away and located near the Galactic Center. It is one of the more metal-rich globular clusters, meaning its stars contain a relatively high proportion of heavy elements from earlier stellar generations. Only 14 variable stars have been identified within it, fewer than in most globulars of similar size.

name: Ptolemy Cluster
description: Ptolemy's Cluster is one of the brightest and largest open clusters in the sky, visible to the naked eye as a glowing patch in Scorpius. It lies about 980 light-years away, spans roughly 25 light-years, and contains around 80 member stars estimated to be 220 million years old. The Greek astronomer Ptolemy recorded it around 130 CE, making it one of the earliest catalogued deep-sky objects.

name: Messier 70
description: Messier 70 is a compact globular cluster in Sagittarius lying about 29,400 light-years away, appearing very similar to its neighbor M69. Like M62, it appears to have undergone core collapse, producing a very high central stellar density. The comet Hale-Bopp was discovered in 1995 just 1 degree from M70 during a routine observation with a moderate-aperture telescope.

name: Messier 71
description: Messier 71 is a loosely concentrated globular cluster in the small constellation Sagitta, about 12,000 light-years away. For many years astronomers debated whether it was an unusually rich open cluster or a true globular; it is now firmly classified as a globular with an unusually sparse core. At about 27 light-years across it is one of the smaller Messier globulars and contains a higher proportion of heavy elements than most.

name: Messier 72
description: Messier 72 is a faint, loosely concentrated globular cluster in Aquarius, about 54,600 light-years away and one of the more remote in the Messier catalog. Its large distance gives it a small apparent size and low surface brightness. It is estimated to be around 9.5 billion years old, somewhat younger than the oldest globulars.

name: Messier 73
description: Messier 73 is simply an asterism, a chance grouping of four unrelated stars in Aquarius that happen to lie near each other in the sky. Messier catalogued it as a cluster of small stars with faint nebulosity, but modern measurements show the stars lie at very different distances and have no physical connection. It remains in the catalog purely for historical completeness.

name: Messier 74
description: The Phantom Galaxy is one of the most symmetrically perfect face-on grand design spiral galaxies known, located about 32 million light-years away in Pisces. Despite its photographic beauty with well-defined spiral arms and active star-forming regions, its low surface brightness makes it notoriously difficult to observe visually and one of the most challenging Messier objects. James Webb Space Telescope images released in 2022 revealed stunning mid-infrared detail in its dust lanes and HII regions.

name: Messier 75
description: Messier 75 is one of the most remote and concentrated globular clusters in the Messier catalog, about 67,500 light-years away in Sagittarius. Around 80 percent of its total luminosity is concentrated in a very tight core, giving it one of the highest central stellar densities of any known globular. It contains an estimated 400,000 stars.

name: Little Dumbbell Nebula
description: The Little Dumbbell Nebula is a small planetary nebula in Perseus about 2,500 light-years away, and the visually faintest object in the entire Messier catalog. Its two bright lobes form a dumbbell or barbell shape, while a dimmer surrounding halo makes it a bipolar nebula viewed nearly side-on. The central white dwarf is one of the hottest known, with a surface temperature estimated around 88,000 Kelvin.

name: Cetus A
description: Messier 77 is the nearest Seyfert galaxy to Earth, lying about 47 million light-years away in Cetus. Its active nucleus houses a supermassive black hole of roughly 15 million solar masses that drives powerful radio emission, earning it the radio-source designation Cetus A. The bright, compact nucleus surrounded by loosely wound spiral arms is visible in medium-aperture telescopes.

name: Messier 78
description: Messier 78 is the brightest diffuse reflection nebula in the sky, glowing with blue-white scattered starlight from two hot embedded stars about 1,350 light-years away in Orion. Part of the vast Orion Molecular Cloud complex, it is filled with young stellar objects and Herbig-Haro jets that betray ongoing star formation. Long exposures connect it to neighbouring reflection nebulae McNeil's Nebula and NGC 2071.

name: Messier 79
description: Messier 79 is a compact globular cluster in Lepus, about 41,000 light-years away, making it one of the few Messier globulars located in the opposite direction from the Galactic Center. It is believed to have originated in the Canis Major Dwarf Galaxy, which is currently being disrupted and absorbed by the Milky Way, and was later captured into a Milky Way orbit. Its concentrated core makes it appear as a bright, condensed ball of light in small telescopes.

name: Lagoon Nebula
description: The Lagoon Nebula is a vast emission nebula in Sagittarius spanning roughly 110 by 50 light-years at a distance of about 4,100 light-years. It is an active star-forming region centred on the open cluster NGC 6530 and energised by a massive hourglass-shaped core lit by the hot star Herschel 36. Long-exposure photographs reveal the nebula in vivid red from hydrogen-alpha emission.

name: Messier 80
description: Messier 80 is one of the densest globular clusters in the Milky Way, containing several hundred thousand stars packed into a sphere about 96 light-years across at a distance of 32,600 light-years in Scorpius. In 1860 a nova briefly flared within it, one of very few novae ever observed in a globular cluster, and the cluster's extraordinary density likely drives the large population of blue straggler stars found here. Its bright, intensely concentrated core makes it one of the most striking globulars in the southern summer sky.

name: Bode's Galaxy
description: Bode's Galaxy is a grand design spiral galaxy about 11.7 million light-years away in Ursa Major and one of the intrinsically brightest galaxies in the sky. It is the dominant member of the M81 Group, a collection of more than 30 galaxies, and its gravitational interaction with the starburst galaxy M82 just 38 arcminutes away has triggered enhanced star formation in both. Its beautifully symmetric, tightly wound spiral arms and luminous nucleus are visible in binoculars from dark sites.

name: Cigar Galaxy
description: The Cigar Galaxy is a starburst galaxy about 11.4 million light-years away in Ursa Major, undergoing an explosive burst of star formation triggered by gravitational interaction with M81. Its central starburst region forms stars at a rate ten times higher than the Milky Way, and supernovae and stellar winds drive a spectacular superwind of ionised gas extending thousands of light-years above and below the disk. In 2014 it hosted SN 2014J, one of the nearest Type Ia supernovae observed in modern times.

name: Southern Pinwheel Galaxy
description: The Southern Pinwheel Galaxy is one of the nearest and most photogenic barred spiral galaxies, about 14.7 million light-years away in Hydra. Its face-on orientation reveals tightly wound spiral arms rich in pink star-forming regions and blue young star clusters. It has hosted six recorded supernovae, more than any other nearby galaxy of comparable size.

name: Messier 84
description: Messier 84 is a massive lenticular galaxy at the heart of the Virgo Cluster, about 60 million light-years away. Its active nucleus harbors a black hole of nearly 900 million solar masses that drives high-velocity radio jets extending far beyond the optical disk. It lies at the core of Markarian's Chain, a visually striking curved alignment of Virgo Cluster galaxies.

name: Messier 85
description: Messier 85 is the northernmost galaxy in the Virgo Cluster, about 60 million light-years away in Coma Berenices, and is undergoing a slow merger with the smaller spiral IC 3292. This ongoing interaction gives M85 an unusually blue outer envelope for an otherwise old lenticular galaxy, a sign of relatively recent star formation stimulated by the merger. It is a bright, oval smudge in small telescopes with a noticeably stellar nucleus.

name: Messier 86
description: Messier 86 is a giant elliptical galaxy in the Virgo Cluster about 52 million light-years away, and one of the few in the cluster with a net blueshift, meaning it is actually moving toward us through the complex Virgo gravitational field. It is among the most X-ray luminous members of the Virgo Cluster, surrounded by an extended halo of hot gas. It lies alongside M84 at the dense core of Markarian's Chain.

name: Virgo A
description: Messier 87 is the dominant giant elliptical galaxy at the center of the Virgo Cluster, about 53 million light-years away, and home to a supermassive black hole of 6.5 billion solar masses. In 2019 it became the first black hole ever directly imaged when the Event Horizon Telescope captured its glowing accretion shadow. The galaxy produces a spectacular relativistic jet of plasma visible across the electromagnetic spectrum, stretching thousands of light-years from its nucleus.

name: Messier 88
description: Messier 88 is one of the brightest spiral galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, lying 47 to 60 million light-years away in Coma Berenices and tilted about 30 degrees from edge-on. Its nucleus shows low-level Seyfert 2 activity, and well-defined dust lanes run along its nearly edge-on disk. Multiple spiral arms and an elongated bright core make it a rewarding target for medium-aperture telescopes.

name: Messier 89
description: Messier 89 is a massive elliptical galaxy in the Virgo Cluster about 50 to 60 million light-years away, appearing nearly circular in most images. Deep X-ray observations reveal radio jets and shells of diffuse material extending far beyond the optical disk, and it hosts over 2,000 globular clusters. Its nearly round appearance and low-luminosity active nucleus make it appear featureless in small telescopes.

name: Messier 9
description: Messier 9 is a compact globular cluster about 25,800 light-years from Earth in Ophiuchus, relatively close to the Galactic Center. Interstellar dust partially dims and reddens its light, giving it a somewhat mottled, brownish appearance in images. The cluster contains roughly 250,000 stars within a diameter of about 90 light-years.

name: Messier 90
description: Messier 90 is a lenticular galaxy in the Virgo Cluster about 58.7 million light-years away, notable as one of only a handful of galaxies with a net blueshift, meaning it is currently moving toward the Milky Way. Ram-pressure stripping as M90 plunges through the cluster's hot intracluster medium is gradually removing its remaining interstellar gas. Despite this, faint traces of spiral structure remain visible in deep images.

name: Messier 91
description: Messier 91 is a barred spiral galaxy in the Virgo Cluster about 63 million light-years away in Coma Berenices. It was a missing Messier object for over two centuries due to an error in Messier's position, finally identified in 1969 by amateur astronomer William C. Williams. Its central bar and tightly wound spiral arms are visible in moderate apertures.

name: Messier 92
description: Messier 92 is one of the finest globular clusters in the northern sky, often overlooked because of its proximity to the more famous M13 just 9 degrees away in Hercules. Lying about 26,700 light-years from Earth, it is one of the oldest globular clusters at an estimated 14.2 billion years, making it older than most of the universe's current age estimates. Its dense, rich core resolves beautifully in medium-aperture telescopes.

name: Messier 93
description: Messier 93 is a bright, rich open cluster of about 80 stars in Puppis, approximately 3,600 light-years away. Its brightest members form a distinctive arrowhead or butterfly shape, dominated by hot blue-white stars. The cluster is around 100 to 130 million years old and lies in a rich Milky Way field.

name: Messier 94
description: Messier 94 is a spiral galaxy in Canes Venatici about 16 million light-years away, notable for an unusually bright and active inner ring of star formation surrounding its compact nucleus. This starburst ring dominates the ultraviolet appearance of the galaxy and contributes a large fraction of its total star-forming activity. Two faint outer ring structures extending well beyond the bright core have been detected in deep images.

name: Messier 95
description: Messier 95 is a barred spiral galaxy in the Leo I Group, about 38 million light-years away in Leo. Its prominent central bar connects to an inner ring from which two main spiral arms emerge, making it a textbook example of a ringed barred spiral galaxy. The supernova SN 2012aw occurred in its disk, briefly reaching 12th magnitude and visible in amateur telescopes.

name: Messier 96
description: Messier 96 is the largest and brightest member of the Leo I Group, a spiral galaxy about 31 million light-years away in Leo. It has an unusually asymmetric spiral structure with one arm more developed than the other, and its nucleus is slightly offset from the disk's geometric center, both features likely caused by past gravitational interactions. Its bright oval glow with a stellar nucleus is visible in small telescopes.

name: Owl Nebula
description: The Owl Nebula is a large, nearly circular planetary nebula in Ursa Major about 2,030 light-years away, one of the largest planetary nebulae in the sky at over 1.8 light-years across. Its name comes from two circular dark patches in long-exposure photographs that resemble the eye sockets of an owl, though these features require a reasonably large aperture to see visually. Its large size gives it a low surface brightness, making it tricky in smaller instruments.

name: Messier 98
description: Messier 98 is a large, nearly edge-on spiral galaxy in Coma Berenices, about 44 million light-years away and a member of the Virgo Cluster. One of the blueshifted Virgo Cluster members, it is approaching the Milky Way at over 140 km per second. Its near-edge-on tilt reveals a prominent dust lane running through a bright elongated nucleus.

name: Coma Pinwheel Galaxy
description: The Coma Pinwheel Galaxy is a nearly face-on grand design spiral in Coma Berenices, about 55 million light-years away and a bright member of the Virgo Cluster. Unusually for a Virgo Cluster galaxy, it has a significant blueshift, approaching at nearly 140 km per second, attributed to peculiar infall motions. Its asymmetric spiral arms and multiple star-forming regions have made it a key laboratory for studying the physics of HII regions.

name: NGC 1022
description: NGC 1022 is a barred spiral galaxy located approximately 68 million light years away in the equatorial constellation of Cetus. It was discovered on September 10, 1785, by William Herschel. NGC 1022 is a member of the Cetus-Aries group of galaxies.

name: NGC 1023
description: NGC 1023 is a barred lenticular galaxy in Perseus, the dominant member of its own small galaxy group, about 36 million light-years away. Its lens-shaped disk with a bright central bar is tilted enough to show a subtle dust lane in deep images. Several dwarf companion galaxies cluster around it, and its halo harbors an unusually rich population of planetary nebulae used for distance measurements.

name: NGC 1027
description: NGC 1027 is an open cluster of about 40 stars in Cassiopeia, roughly 3,100 light-years away, forming a scattered grouping around a bright orange giant star that stands out prominently. It is estimated to be around 100 million years old. Its loose arrangement is best appreciated at low magnification in a wide field.

name: 47 Tucanae
description: 47 Tucanae is the second brightest globular cluster in the sky and the finest in the southern hemisphere after Omega Centauri, lying about 14,850 light-years away on the outskirts of the Small Magellanic Cloud in Tucana. Despite its apparent proximity to the SMC it is about 60,000 light-years closer, lying in the Milky Way's halo. Its dense, rich core resolves into hundreds of individual stars in any telescope, and it contains a remarkable concentration of millisecond pulsars thought to form through stellar collisions in its dense interior.

name: NGC 1052
description: NGC 1052 is an elliptical galaxy in the constellation Cetus. It was discovered on January 10, 1785 by the astronomer William Herschel. It is a member of the eponymous NGC 1052 Group.

name: NGC 1055
description: NGC 1055 is a large edge-on spiral galaxy in Cetus about 60 million light-years away, a companion to the Cetus A galaxy M77. Deep images reveal a warped outer disk and extensive extraplanar dust, suggesting a past gravitational interaction. Its boxy central bulge and prominent dust lane make it a classic edge-on target for imagers working in the NGC 1068 field.

name: NGC 1084
description: NGC 1084 is a bright spiral galaxy in Eridanus about 60 million light-years away, known for an above-average supernova rate with six recorded events in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. It has a moderately inclined disk with active star-forming regions scattered through its arms. Its relative isolation in the sky makes it a straightforward imaging target.

name: NGC 1232
description: NGC 1232 is a grand design face-on spiral galaxy in Eridanus about 50 million light-years away, its beautifully symmetric multiple spiral arms richly dotted with bright blue star-forming knots and pink HII regions. A small irregular companion galaxy NGC 1232A to the east distorts one of its outer arms slightly through gravitational interaction. Its large apparent size and face-on orientation make it one of the most detailed spiral galaxies accessible to moderate-aperture imagers in the winter sky.

name: NGC 1245
description: NGC 1245 is an open cluster in the constellation Perseus. It was discovered by William Herschel on 11 December 1786.

name: NGC 129
description: NGC 129 is an open cluster in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was discovered by William Herschel in 1788.

name: NGC 1300
description: NGC 1300 is considered one of the finest examples of a grand barred spiral galaxy in the sky, about 61 million light-years away in Eridanus. Its sweeping bar structure extends across two-thirds of the galaxy's total diameter, with the two main spiral arms emerging gracefully from the tips of the bar. Hubble imagery has revealed a secondary nucleus-within-nucleus structure suggesting a recent minor merger.

name: NGC 134
description: NGC 134 is a barred spiral galaxy that resembles the Milky Way with its spiral arms loosely wrapped around a bright, bar-shaped central region. Its loosely bound spiral arms categorize it as Hubble-type Sbc.

name: NGC 1342
description: NGC 1342, sometimes also known as the Stingray Cluster, is an open cluster in the constellation Perseus. It was discovered by William Herschel on 28 December 1799.

name: NGC 136
description: NGC 136 is an open cluster in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was discovered by William Herschel on November 26, 1788.

name: Robin's Egg Nebula
description: NGC 1360 is a large, elliptical planetary nebula in Fornax, known as the Robin's Egg Nebula for its smooth blue-green oval of ionized oxygen. It is older and more diffuse than a typical planetary nebula and has a hot binary star at its centre. At about 1,150 light-years away it is bright enough to show colour in modest telescopes.

name: Great Barred Spiral Galaxy
description: The Great Barred Spiral Galaxy is one of the largest and most spectacular barred spirals in the nearby universe, lying about 56 million light-years away in Fornax. Its two main arms emerge from the ends of a bar roughly 86,000 light-years long, carrying active star-forming regions and luminous blue clusters. It hosts a Seyfert 1.5 active nucleus containing a black hole that is spinning at close to the maximum rate allowed by general relativity.

name: NGC 1380
description: NGC 1380 is a lenticular galaxy located in the constellation Fornax. It is located at a distance of about 60 million light years from Earth, which, given its apparent dimensions, means that NGC 1380 is about 85,000 light years across.

name: NGC 1407
description: NGC 1407 is an elliptical galaxy in Eridanus. It is at a distance of 76 million light-years from Earth.

name: Maia Nebula
description: Maia, designated 20 Tauri, is a star in the constellation of Taurus. It is a blue giant of spectral type B8 III, a chemically peculiar star.

name: Merope Nebula
description: The Merope Nebula is a diffuse reflection nebula in the Pleiades star cluster, surrounding the 4th magnitude star Merope. It was discovered on October 19, 1859 by the German astronomer Wilhelm Tempel.

name: NGC 1444
description: NGC 1444 is a small open cluster of stars in the northern constellation of Perseus, about 2-1⁄4° to the northwest of 43 Persei. The cluster has sixty members of seventh magnitude or fainter, and is better appreciated in larger telescopes.

name: Fossil Footprint Nebula
description: NGC 1491 is a bright emission nebula and H II region in Perseus, also called the Fossil Footprint Nebula. A hot, luminous central star is blowing a bubble in the surrounding hydrogen, pushing the gas into a sharp rim on one side and a darker cavity behind it. The strong contrast between the ionized edge and the dust around it makes it a popular narrowband target. It lies roughly 10,000 light-years away.

name: California Nebula
description: The California Nebula is a large emission nebula in Perseus, roughly 1,500 light-years away, whose elongated outline resembles the shape of the US state of California. It is ionised by Xi Persei (Menkib), a hot O7 supergiant that lies nearby but is not physically embedded in the nebula. Its low surface brightness makes it effectively invisible visually but spectacular in hydrogen-alpha photographs.

name: NGC 1501
description: NGC 1501 is a planetary nebula with a complex structure, located in the northern constellation of Camelopardalis. It has the proper names Camel's Eye Nebula and the Oyster Nebula.

name: NGC 1502
description: NGC 1502 is a young open cluster of approximately 60 stars in the constellation Camelopardalis, discovered by William Herschel on November 3, 1787.

name: NGC 1513
description: NGC 1513 is an open cluster of stars in the northern constellation of Perseus, positioned 2° SSE of the faint star Lambda Persei. The same telescope field contains the clusters NGC 1528 and NGC 1545.

name: NGC 1528
description: NGC 1528 is a rich open cluster of about 200 stars in Perseus, roughly 2,500 light-years away, with an estimated age of around 370 million years. It is a large cluster with a notably wide spread of stellar luminosities and several red giant members. The cluster makes a fine binocular object in the same region as the famous Double Cluster.

name: NGC 1531
description: NGC 1531 is a dwarf galaxy in the constellation Eridanus that is interacting with the larger spiral galaxy NGC 1532. It was discovered by John Herschel on 19 October 1835.

name: NGC 1532
description: NGC 1532, also known as Haley's Coronet, is an edge-on barred spiral galaxy located approximately 58 million light-years from the Solar System in the constellation Eridanus. The galaxy was discovered by James Dunlop on 29 October 1826.

name: Cleopatra's Eye
description: Cleopatra's Eye is a bright planetary nebula in Eridanus about 6,000 light-years away, displaying a striking double-shell structure with a bright inner disk surrounded by a fainter outer halo. The inner disk has a vivid blue-green colour in photographs from ionised oxygen, while the faint outer shell is seen in hydrogen-alpha. Its small angular size requires a moderate telescope to resolve its disk from a star.

name: NGC 1545
description: NGC 1545 is an open cluster in the constellation Perseus. It was discovered by William Herschel on December 28, 1790.

name: Northern Trifid Nebula
description: NGC 1579, the Northern Trifid, is an emission and reflection nebula in Perseus about 2,100 light-years away, visually resembling the Trifid Nebula (M20) with similar dark lane divisions and a mix of red and blue nebular colours. It is associated with the young star LkH-alpha 101, a luminous Herbig Ae/Be star embedded within the cloud. Long-exposure narrowband images reveal rich filamentary structure across several light-years.

name: NGC 1647
description: NGC 1647 is an open cluster in the constellation Taurus. It contains nearly 90 stars and it lies at a distance of 550 parsec.

name: NGC 1664
description: NGC 1664 is an open cluster in the constellation of Auriga. It contains stars with a total of around 640 solar masses with a tidal radius of 43 ly (13.2 pc).

name: NGC 1788
description: The Cosmic Bat is a mixed emission and reflection nebula in Orion about 1,350 light-years away, its dark wing-like shape of absorbing dust giving the appearance of a bat in flight. The nebula is lit partly by reflection off dust and partly by embedded young stars, and it sits within the larger Orion Molecular Cloud complex. Deep images reveal it to be a rich nursery of newly forming stars invisible at optical wavelengths.

name: NGC 1817
description: NGC 1817 is an open cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus. It was discovered by English astronomer William Herschel in February 1784.

name: NGC 1857
description: NGC 1857 is an open cluster in the constellation Auriga, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 7, spanning about 5 arcminutes, it is an easy target for small telescopes.

name: NGC 1893
description: NGC 1893 is a young open cluster in Auriga, about 12,400 light-years away, associated with the emission nebula IC 410 and its famous pair of cometary globules called the Tadpoles. The hot young O-type stars in the cluster ionise the surrounding nebula and are sculpting the Tadpole pillars through photoevaporation. In narrowband images the nebula glows vividly around the centrally concentrated cluster.

name: NGC 1907
description: NGC 1907 is an open star cluster around 5,200 light years from Earth. It contains around 300 stars and is around 500 million years old. With a magnitude of 8.2, it is visible in the constellation Auriga.

name: Fly Nebula
description: The Fly Nebula is a compact emission and reflection nebula in Auriga, about 7,000 light-years away, surrounding a tight cluster of four young hot stars embedded within. Its glowing core is rich in ionised hydrogen, with a faint surrounding reflection halo visible in deep images. Though small in angular size, it is a bright enough compact target to resolve structure in moderate apertures.

name: NGC 1961
description: NGC 1961 is a spiral galaxy in the constellation Camelopardalis. It was discovered by German-British astronomer William Herschel on 3 December 1788.

name: NGC 1964
description: NGC 1964 is a barred spiral galaxy in the constellation Lepus. The galaxy lies 65 million light years away from Earth, which means, given its apparent dimensions, that NGC 1964 is approximately 150,000 light years across.

name: Running Man Nebula
description: Sh 2-279 is an HII region and bright nebulae that includes a reflection nebula located in the constellation Orion. The reflection nebula embedded in Sh 2-279 is popularly known as the Running Man Nebula.

name: NGC 1980
description: NGC 1980 is an open cluster and associated reflection nebulosity in Orion, about 1,340 light-years away, physically close to and often considered part of the greater Orion Nebula complex. Its dominant star is Iota Orionis, the southernmost star of Orion's sword, a massive O-type binary that illuminates the surrounding cloud. The combination of bright stellar association and rich surrounding nebulosity makes it a natural wide-field companion to M42.

name: NGC 1999
description: NGC 1999 is a compact reflection nebula in Orion about 1,500 light-years away, famous for a distinctive dark circular hole in its nebulosity that was initially misidentified as a Bok globule. Herschel Space Observatory infrared observations later revealed the dark patch is actually a true void in the gas and dust, likely blown clear by outflows from the young stellar object V380 Orionis at the nebula's center. It sits in the rich Orion Molecular Cloud and is surrounded by numerous Herbig-Haro jet flows.

name: NGC 2022
description: It was first observed by William Herschel on December 28, 1785, who described it as: considerably bright, nearly round, like a star with a large diameter, like an ill-defined planetary nebula. In medium-sized amateur telescopes it looks like a small grayish patch of light.

name: Flame Nebula
description: The Flame Nebula is a striking emission nebula in Orion, about 1,350 light-years away, lit from within by the multiple star system Alnitak (Zeta Orionis). Dark dust lanes carved by stellar winds divide the glowing gas into bright lobes resembling flames. It sits just east of Alnitak and forms a natural pair with the Horsehead Nebula in the same wide-field field of view.

name: NGC 2126
description: NGC 2126 is an open cluster in the constellation Auriga, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. It spans about 5 arcminutes.

name: NGC 2129
description: NGC 2129 is an open cluster in the constellation Gemini. NGC 2129 is a very young cluster whose age has been estimated at 10 million years.

name: NGC 2158
description: NGC 2158, also known as OCL 468, Lund 206 or Melotte 40, it is an open cluster of stars located around 11,000 light years from Earth in the constellation of Gemini. It is of intermediate age being around 2 billion years old.

name: 37 Cluster
description: NGC 2169, nicknamed the 37 Cluster, is a small but striking open cluster in Orion about 3,600 light-years away, whose brightest members trace a number that looks remarkably like the numerals 3 and 7. Consisting of roughly 30 stars, it is a young cluster of around 8 million years old dominated by hot blue B-type stars. It is a rewarding and unusual target at medium magnification.

name: Angel Nebula
description: NGC 2170 is a bright reflection nebula in Monoceros, part of the Mon R2 star-forming complex about 2,400 light-years away. It is one of several nebulae in a rich cluster of reflection and emission patches in this region, glowing blue from the scattered light of an embedded young stellar cluster. The surrounding area contains multiple overlapping nebulae that create a complex and photogenic wide-field target.

name: Monkey Head Nebula
description: The Monkey Head Nebula is an emission nebula in Orion about 6,400 light-years away, ionised by a young open cluster at its center. Its curved, sculpted pillars and irregular rim resemble the profile of a monkey's head and are formed by the erosive ultraviolet light of the embedded hot stars. It is a popular narrowband imaging target, glowing vividly in hydrogen-alpha with blue OIII highlights.

name: NGC 2186
description: NGC 2186 is an open cluster in the constellation Orion, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 8.7, spanning about 4 arcminutes, it is a modest target for amateur telescopes.

name: NGC 2194
description: NGC 2194 is an open cluster in the constellation Orion. The cluster is located about 10,000 light years away from Earth. It is rich and moderately concentrated. The cluster lies 33 arcminutes west-northwest of 73 Orionis.

name: NGC 2204
description: NGC 2204 is an open cluster of stars in the Canis Major constellation. It was discovered by the German-English astronomer William Herschel on 6 February 1785.

name: NGC 2207
description: NGC 2207 and IC 2163 are a pair of colliding spiral galaxies about 80 million light-years away in the constellation Canis Major. NGC 2207 was discovered by British astronomer John Herschel on 24 January 1835, while IC 2163 was discovered by Herbert Howe on 11 February 1898.

name: NGC 2215
description: NGC 2215 is an open cluster in the constellation Monoceros, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 8.45, spanning about 8 arcminutes, it is a modest target for amateur telescopes.

name: NGC 2232
description: NGC 2232 is a bright open star cluster in the equatorial constellation of Monoceros, centered on the star 10 Monocerotis. It is located in the Gould Belt close to the Orion Nebula cluster, at a mean distance of 1,060 ly from the Sun.

name: Rosette Nebula
description: The Rosette Nebula is a vast circular emission nebula in Monoceros, about 5,200 light-years away, enclosing the open cluster NGC 2244 at its core. The ring of glowing gas spans roughly 130 light-years and is one of the most recognised astrophotography targets in the sky. Radiation and stellar winds from the central cluster have blown a clear cavity in the nebula's centre, pushing the gas outward into the rose-like pattern.

name: Rosette Cluster
description: NGC 2244 is the brilliant young open cluster at the centre of the Rosette Nebula, containing about 200 stars formed from the surrounding molecular cloud roughly 4 million years ago. The most massive members are luminous O-type giants whose ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds carved the central cavity of the Rosette Nebula and still power its glowing gas. At low magnification the cluster is a striking loose scattering of bright blue-white stars set against the glowing nebular backdrop.

name: NGC 225
description: NGC 225 is an open cluster in the constellation Cassiopeia. It is located roughly 2,200 light-years from Earth. It is about 100 to 150 million years old.

name: NGC 2251
description: NGC 2251 is an open cluster in the constellation Monoceros, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 7.3, spanning about 6 arcminutes, it is an easy target for small telescopes.

name: Cone Nebula / Christmas Tree
description: The Christmas Tree Cluster and Cone Nebula form a combined object in Monoceros about 2,500 light-years away. Seen with south upward, the cluster's stars trace an upright Christmas tree shape, with the bright star S Monocerotis at its base. The Cone Nebula at the cluster's tip is a dark pillar of dense molecular gas being eroded by ultraviolet light from the hot cluster stars, visible in deep narrowband photographs.

name: NGC 2266
description: NGC 2266 is an open cluster of stars in the constellation of Gemini. It was discovered by German-British astronomer William Herschel on 7 December 1785.

name: NGC 2281
description: NGC 2281, also known as the Broken Heart Cluster, is an open cluster of stars in the northern constellation of Auriga. It was discovered by English astronomer William Herschel on March 4, 1788, and described as a, "cluster of coarsely scattered pretty [bright] stars, pretty rich".

name: NGC 2286
description: NGC 2286 is an open cluster in the constellation Monoceros, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 7.5, spanning about 5 arcminutes, it is an easy target for small telescopes.

name: Great Bird Cluster
description: NGC 2301 is a bright and well-concentrated open cluster in Monoceros about 2,500 light-years away, sometimes nicknamed Hagrid's Dragon for the shape formed by its brightest members. It contains around 80 confirmed members dominated by hot blue-white stars with an estimated age of around 150 million years. Its compact, rich core makes it a rewarding sight in any telescope.

name: NGC 2304
description: NGC 2304 is an open cluster in the constellation Gemini, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 10, spanning about 5 arcminutes, it is a modest target for amateur telescopes.

name: NGC 2311
description: NGC 2311 is an open cluster in the constellation Monoceros, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 9.6, spanning about 6 arcminutes, it is a modest target for amateur telescopes.

name: NGC 2324
description: NGC 2324 is an open cluster in the constellation Monoceros, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 8.4, spanning about 9 arcminutes, it is a modest target for amateur telescopes.

name: NGC 2335
description: NGC 2335 is an open cluster in the constellation Monoceros, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 7.2, spanning about 9 arcminutes, it is an easy target for small telescopes.

name: NGC 2343
description: NGC 2343 is an open cluster in the constellation Monoceros, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 6.7, spanning about 8 arcminutes, it is an easy target for small telescopes.

name: NGC 2353
description: NGC 2353 is an open cluster of about 30 stars in Monoceros, roughly 3,000 light-years away, and estimated to be around 80 million years old. It is centred on an orange giant star that provides a warm color anchor in a field of mostly blue-white members. The cluster sits in a rich Milky Way field near the Monoceros star-forming complex.

name: NGC 2354
description: NGC 2354 is an open cluster in the constellation Canis Major. It lies 2 degrees southwest from NGC 2362 and northeast of Delta Canis Majoris. About 15 member stars are visible through binoculars.

name: NGC 2355
description: NGC 2355 also known as NGC 2356, is an old open cluster in the constellation Gemini.

name: Thor's Helmet
description: Thor's Helmet is a spectacular wind-blown emission nebula in Canis Major about 11,960 light-years away, shaped by the powerful stellar wind from the Wolf-Rayet star WR 7 at its center. The central bubble is flanked by two wing-like extensions that give the nebula its iconic helmet shape. In narrowband photographs its complex interacting shells of ionised gas glow in vivid hydrogen-alpha, nitrogen, and oxygen emission.

name: NGC 2371
description: NGC 2371-2 is a dual lobed planetary nebula located in the constellation Gemini.

name: Eskimo Nebula
description: The Eskimo Nebula (also called the Clown Face Nebula) is a bright double-shell planetary nebula in Gemini about 2,870 light-years away. Its inner disk is surrounded by a complex outer ring of comet-like filaments that resemble a parka hood viewed from the front, giving it the Eskimo nickname. Hubble Space Telescope images revealed the inner disk to be a pair of expanding gas streams rather than a simple shell.

name: NGC 2395
description: NGC 2395 is an open cluster in the constellation Gemini, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 8, spanning about 5 arcminutes, it is an easy target for small telescopes.

name: NGC 2420
description: NGC 2420 is an open cluster in the constellation Gemini. It was discovered by German-British astronomer William Herschel on 19 November 1783. The cluster is about two billion years old and it is located 10,000 light years away.

name: NGC 2421
description: NGC 2421 is an open cluster in the constellation Puppis, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 8.3, spanning about 5 arcminutes, it is a modest target for amateur telescopes.

name: NGC 2423
description: NGC 2423 is an open cluster in the constellation Puppis, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 6.7, spanning about 12 arcminutes, it is an easy target for small telescopes.

name: NGC 2438
description: NGC 2438 is a planetary nebula in the southern constellation of Puppis. Parallax measurements by Gaia put the central star at a distance of roughly 1,370 light years.

name: NGC 2440
description: NGC 2440 is a bright, compact bipolar planetary nebula in Puppis about 3,600 light-years away, surrounding one of the hottest known white dwarf stars with a surface temperature near 200,000 Kelvin. Its complex, multi-lobed structure in Hubble images reveals overlapping shells from multiple mass-loss episodes during the star's red giant phase. Despite its relatively small angular size, it is bright enough to show a non-stellar disk in moderate telescopes under high magnification.

name: NGC 2451
description: NGC 2451 is an open cluster in the Puppis constellation, probably discovered by Giovanni Battista Hodierna before 1654 and John Herschel in 1835. In 1994, it was postulated that this was actually two open clusters that lie along the same line of sight.

name: Skull Nebula
description: The Skull Nebula is a large, faint planetary nebula in Cetus about 1,600 light-years away, its irregular circular outline with dark patches and multiple embedded stars evoking a skull in wide-field photographs. It is one of the nearest planetary nebulae to Earth and is notable for its central star being part of a true triple star system. Its low surface brightness demands dark skies and a medium-aperture telescope for a good visual impression, but it is accessible to narrowband imaging.

name: Skull and Crossbones Nebula
description: NGC 2467 is an emission nebula and active star-forming region in Puppis, sometimes called the Skull and Crossbones Nebula for the face-like shape its bright central cavity and surrounding dust form in wide-field images. What looks like a single cluster is really several groups of young stars at different distances along the same line of sight. The main nebula lies roughly 13,000 light-years away.

name: NGC 2479
description: NGC 2479 is an open cluster in the constellation Puppis, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 9.6, spanning about 6 arcminutes, it is a modest target for amateur telescopes.

name: NGC 2482
