It has well-developed, symmetric spiral arms and a relatively compact nucleus. It is a member of a small galaxy group and forms a visual trio with NGC 5353 and NGC 5354 in wide-field images.

name: NGC5985
description: NGC 5985 is a barred spiral galaxy in Draco about 130 million light-years away and part of a visual grouping with NGC 5982 and NGC 5981. The three galaxies display three different orientations: face-on, inclined, and edge-on, making this compact trio a classic demonstration of galaxy inclination in a single photographic field. NGC 5985 itself shows a prominent bar and open spiral arms.

name: Rim Nebula
description: The Fighting Dragons of Ara is a dramatic emission nebula in Ara about 4,000 light-years away, sculpted by the young open cluster NGC 6193 at its centre. The dark dust pillars and bright ionised rims formed by the cluster's ultraviolet radiation create the impression of mythological dragons in combat in wide-field narrowband photographs. It is one of the finest narrowband imaging targets in the southern sky.

name: NGC6503
description: NGC 6503 is an isolated dwarf spiral galaxy in Draco about 17 million light-years away, sitting in the Local Void, a vast region of space largely empty of galaxies. Its relative isolation from major galaxy groups makes it an excellent laboratory for studying spiral galaxy evolution without environmental influences. Its thin blue disk with numerous HII regions and pinkish star-forming knots make it a photogenic spring target.

name: NGC6820
description: NGC 6820 is an emission nebula in Vulpecula about 6,000 light-years away, surrounding and ionised by the young open cluster NGC 6823 at its center. Its most striking feature is a prominent pillar or trunk of dense molecular gas pointing toward the hot cluster stars, sculpted by their ultraviolet radiation. In narrowband images it reveals a complex mixture of emission and dark nebular structure.

name: Blinking Planetary
description: The Blinking Planetary is a small, bright planetary nebula in Cygnus about 2,200 light-years away, famous for a striking visual illusion: when you look directly at the central star the surrounding nebulosity seems to disappear, reappearing when you use averted vision. This blinking effect results from the high contrast between the bright central star and the fainter surrounding shell. It is a satisfying object even in small telescopes.

name: Fireworks Galaxy
description: The Fireworks Galaxy is a face-on spiral galaxy in Cepheus about 22.5 million light-years away, near the border with Cygnus. It has hosted ten observed supernovae in the past century, the highest recorded rate of any known galaxy, earning it its explosive nickname. Its numerous pink star-forming regions and blue young clusters are well resolved in photographs, and its location within the Milky Way plane means it peers through a rich foreground of Milky Way stars.

name: NGC7006
description: NGC 7006 is a remote globular cluster in Delphinus, about 135,000 light-years from Earth, one of the most distant globular clusters in the Milky Way halo. It orbits far out in the galactic halo on a retrograde orbit, leading some astronomers to suggest it was once a member of a now-disrupted satellite galaxy. Despite its extreme distance, it is still visible as a fuzzy star in moderate-aperture telescopes.

name: Superman Galaxy
description: NGC 7479 (the Superman Galaxy) is a strongly barred spiral galaxy in Pegasus about 105 million light-years away, whose central bar and two main spiral arms create an S-shape that resembles the Superman emblem. Its bar is unusually long and straight relative to its disk size, and its active nucleus hosts a radio jet visible in centimetre-wave observations. It is one of the most striking barred spirals accessible to amateur imaging in the autumn sky.

name: Copeland's Blue Snowball
description: The Blue Snowball is a bright, compact planetary nebula in Andromeda about 2,500 light-years away, easily recognised in any telescope by its vivid blue-green colour from doubly ionised oxygen emission. Its inner shell is surrounded by a fainter outer halo visible in longer exposures. Its small size means it appears nearly star-like at low power, requiring magnification to reveal its disk.

name: NGC188
description: NGC 188 is one of the oldest known open clusters, lying about 5,400 light-years away in Cepheus. Estimated to be around 6.8 billion years old, it has retained its membership through an unusually high fraction of binary stars that resist the gravitational disruption that disperses younger clusters. Its members are dominated by evolved red and yellow giant stars rather than the hot blue-white stars typical of younger clusters.

name: Bow-Tie nebula
description: The Bow-Tie Nebula (NGC 40) is a bright planetary nebula in Cepheus about 3,500 light-years away, whose elongated double-lobed structure is visible in deep images. Its central white dwarf is one of the coolest known for a planetary nebula, with a surface temperature of only around 50,000 Kelvin. The nebula's reddish color in photographs comes primarily from ionized nitrogen and hydrogen emission.

name: NGC4236
description: NGC 4236 is a large, low-surface-brightness barred spiral galaxy in Draco about 15 million light-years away, a member of the M81 Group. Its extremely diffuse disk spans nearly 23 arcminutes on the sky but is so faint it challenges moderate apertures. The galaxy's massive disk of neutral hydrogen extends well beyond its visible stellar population, and it has few conspicuous HII regions despite its grand scale.

name: NGC559
description: NGC 559 is a moderately rich open cluster in Cassiopeia about 3,700 light-years away, containing around 150 member stars. It lies in a rich Milky Way field, and its estimated age of roughly 160 million years places it in middle age for an open cluster. Several slightly evolved yellow stars are mixed in with the cluster's dominant blue-white population.

name: NGC7243
description: NGC 7243 is a sparse open cluster in Lacerta about 2,800 light-years away, containing roughly 40 brighter members spread across an area about 1 degree wide. Its stars are loosely arranged, making it a sweeping low-magnification binocular object. The cluster is estimated to be around 100 million years old, with several slightly evolved yellow and orange stars among its mostly blue-white membership.

name: NGC147
description: NGC 147 is a dwarf elliptical galaxy about 2.53 million light-years away in Cassiopeia, a satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy. It lies close in the sky to its companion dwarf NGC 185 and is gravitationally bound to it, the two galaxies forming the only known dwarf galaxy binary system in the Local Group. Unlike NGC 185, NGC 147 shows no current star formation and no detectable dust, suggesting it stopped forming stars at an earlier epoch.

name: NGC185
description: NGC 185 is a dwarf elliptical galaxy about 2.05 million light-years away in Cassiopeia and a satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy, paired in the sky with the nearly identical NGC 147. Unlike most dwarf ellipticals, it contains a small population of relatively young stars and a nuclear concentration of dust, indicating that some star formation has occurred within the last billion years. A carbon star population gives its nucleus an unusually warm color compared with NGC 147.

name: NGC2419
description: The Intergalactic Wanderer (NGC 2419) is one of the most remote globular clusters in the Milky Way halo, lying about 300,000 light-years from the Galactic Center in Lynx, nearly as far as the Magellanic Clouds. Its great distance makes it a test case for dark matter models and the outer limit of the Milky Way's gravitational reach. Despite its immense distance, it is one of the most massive Milky Way globulars, containing around one million stars.

name: NGC752
description: NGC 752 is a large, scattered open cluster in Andromeda about 1,300 light-years away, containing around 60 confirmed member stars spread across a wide area best suited to binoculars or a rich-field telescope at low power. At an estimated age of 1.1 to 1.4 billion years, it is one of the older open clusters known to have retained a coherent membership. Several evolved red giant stars are present, making it useful for stellar evolution studies of intermediate-age clusters.

name: NGC4889
description: NGC 4889 is the brightest and most massive galaxy in the Coma Cluster, about 308 million light-years away in Coma Berenices. It harbors one of the most massive known black holes, with a mass estimated between 6 and 37 billion solar masses, and is surrounded by a huge system of globular clusters numbering in the tens of thousands. As one of the most intrinsically luminous elliptical galaxies known, it is often paired with the nearby NGC 4874 to define the center of the enormous Coma Cluster.

name: NGC6885
description: NGC 6885 is a sparse open cluster in Vulpecula about 1,900 light-years away, centered near the yellow supergiant star 20 Vulpeculae. The cluster contains roughly 30 to 40 confirmed members spread across a loose, irregular pattern best appreciated at low magnification. Its estimated age of around 350 million years is consistent with the evolved, slightly cooler supergiants visible among its membership.

name: NGC3626
description: NGC 3626 is a lenticular galaxy in Leo about 70 million light-years away, notable for its counter-rotating gas disk: the interstellar gas in the inner disk rotates in the opposite direction to the galaxy's stars. This counter-rotation is a signature of gas acquired from an external source, likely a cannibalized dwarf galaxy in the relatively recent past. A modest ring of star formation has been triggered by this accreted gas, giving the nucleus a slightly bluer color than typical for a lenticular.

name: Hyades
description: The Hyades is the nearest open cluster to Earth at about 153 light-years, forming the V-shaped head of Taurus and easily visible to the naked eye. With an age of roughly 625 million years it is one of the best-studied intermediate-age clusters, providing a cornerstone for calibrating the stellar distance scale. The bright orange star Aldebaran appears to belong to the cluster but is actually an unrelated foreground star just 65 light-years from Earth.

name: Hubble's Nebula
description: Hubble's Variable Nebula (NGC 2261) is a fan-shaped reflection and emission nebula in Monoceros about 2,500 light-years away, associated with the young variable star R Monocerotis at its tip. The nebula changes its shape and brightness over weeks to months as dense condensations in the surrounding gas cloud cast moving shadows onto the illuminated fan, making it one of very few nebulae that visibly changes on human timescales. It was the first object photographed through the 200-inch Hale Telescope at Palomar when it opened in 1949.

name: NGC6934
description: NGC 6934 is a moderately bright globular cluster in Delphinus about 52,000 light-years from Earth. Its outer regions are well resolved into individual stars in moderate apertures, while the core remains concentrated and unresolved. With an estimated age of around 10 billion years, it is a member of the Milky Way's old halo population.

name: NGC2775
description: NGC 2775 is a bright early-type spiral galaxy in Cancer about 55 million light-years away, displaying a very smooth outer disk and a slightly chaotic inner spiral structure visible in deep images. It has an unusually large and luminous nucleus relative to its disk, suggesting its spiral arms have been largely exhausted of gas through past star formation. A handful of dwarf companion galaxies orbit nearby in the Cancer I Group.

name: IC1613
description: IC 1613 is a dwarf irregular galaxy about 2.38 million light-years away in Cetus, a member of the Local Group notable for its almost complete lack of interstellar dust. Because of this clean sightline, Cepheid variable stars in IC 1613 have been used extensively to calibrate the extragalactic distance scale with minimal extinction correction. Its low surface brightness makes it challenging visually but accessible to narrowband imaging systems looking for its scattered clumps of young stars and HII regions.

name: NGC4697
description: NGC 4697 is a bright elliptical galaxy in Virgo about 54 million light-years away, notable for harboring an unusually large population of X-ray binary systems detected by the Chandra X-ray Observatory. Studies of its planetary nebulae population have provided one of the most precise kinematic measurements of a giant elliptical galaxy halo, showing evidence for a dark matter halo extending well beyond the optical body. It is one of the brighter ellipticals outside the Virgo Cluster proper.

name: NGC2506
description: NGC 2506 is a rich, compact old open cluster in Monoceros about 10,700 light-years away, containing several hundred stars. Its estimated age of around 1.5 to 2 billion years makes it one of the older open clusters known to have survived dynamical disruption. The cluster's main-sequence turnoff at evolved subgiant stars makes it a useful reference point for stellar isochrone calibrations.

name: Caroline's Cluster
description: NGC 2360 is a rich, moderately concentrated open cluster in Canis Major about 3,700 light-years away, containing roughly 80 confirmed members. Its estimated age of around one billion years makes it relatively old for an open cluster, and several evolved red giant members stand out against the predominantly blue-white stars. At low to moderate magnification it is a distinctive compressed grouping in a rich Milky Way field.

name: Jupiter's Ghost Nebula
description: The Ghost of Jupiter (NGC 3242) is a bright, roundish planetary nebula in Hydra about 1,400 light-years away, named for its resemblance in a small telescope to a gas giant planet with a slightly oval, blue-green disk. Its concentric shells of ionized gas include a bright inner oval and a fainter outer halo discovered in deeper imaging, and a pair of faint ansae similar to the Saturn Nebula extend from its outer halo. At roughly 2 arcminutes across, it is large enough to show obvious disk morphology even in modest apertures at medium magnification.

name: NGC247
description: NGC 247 is a moderately inclined dwarf spiral galaxy in Cetus about 11.1 million light-years away, a member of the Sculptor Group. It is famous for a prominent dark void region in its northern disk with no detectable star formation, and its large apparent size of over 20 arcminutes and low surface brightness make it a photographic rather than a visual target. Cepheid variable stars in NGC 247 have been used to refine the distance to the Sculptor Group.

name: NGC2362
description: NGC 2362 is a compact, bright young open cluster in Canis Major about 5,000 light-years away, centered on the luminous fourth-magnitude blue supergiant Tau Canis Majoris. At only about 4 to 5 million years old it is one of the youngest known open clusters, and nearly all of its hot blue-white members are still descending the main sequence from their formation. Its tight, compressed appearance at low magnification makes it one of the most striking young clusters in the winter sky.

name: NGC5694
description: NGC 5694 is a compact, distant globular cluster in Hydra about 113,000 light-years from the Galactic Center, at the extreme outer fringe of the Milky Way halo. Studies of its radial velocity and orbit suggest it may be a captured interloper from an accreted dwarf galaxy, as its retrograde orbit is dynamically inconsistent with a native Milky Way globular. Its great distance makes it unresolvable in all but the largest amateur telescopes.

name: NGC1097
description: NGC 1097 is a large, bright barred spiral galaxy in Fornax about 45 million light-years away, known for its distinct four-armed structure and an unusually prominent nuclear ring of active star formation surrounding a low-luminosity active galactic nucleus. Four narrow linear features extending far beyond the main disk were detected in deep images and are thought to be optical jets from an accreted satellite galaxy, a rare example of optical jet detection in a non-blazar host. It forms an interacting pair with the dwarf elliptical NGC 1097A, which orbits well within its outer disk.

name: NGC6729
description: NGC 6729 is a small variable reflection and emission nebula in Corona Australis about 430 light-years away, one of the nearest active star-forming regions to Earth. Its brightness and shape change noticeably over days to weeks as the embedded pre-main-sequence star R Coronae Australis varies in brightness, making it one of the few objects in the sky that visibly evolves on human timescales. The nebula is part of the densely studied Corona Australis Molecular Cloud, which contains numerous Herbig-Haro objects and T Tauri stars.

name: NGC2477
description: NGC 2477 is one of the richest and most densely packed open clusters in the sky, lying about 4,200 light-years away in Puppis and containing around 300 resolved member stars. At an estimated age of roughly 700 million years it is a relatively old open cluster, and its stars are sufficiently evolved that red and orange giant members are prominent among the fainter blue-white population. It has been compared favorably to the richest globular clusters in terms of star density visible in a single low-magnification field.

name: NGC55
description: NGC 55 is a large, nearly edge-on irregular or Magellanic-type spiral galaxy in Sculptor about 6.4 million light-years away, a companion to NGC 300 in the Sculptor Group. Its highly elongated profile is studded with luminous blue star-forming regions and giant HII complexes that rival the largest in the Local Group, making it one of the few nearby galaxies where individual stellar associations are directly resolved in photographs. Its asymmetric stellar distribution and active star-forming west end suggest recent gravitational interaction with NGC 300.

name: NGC1851
description: NGC 1851 is a bright, compact globular cluster in Columba about 39,000 light-years away, notable for hosting two distinct stellar populations with different ages and chemical compositions separated by only about one billion years. This double population is one of the best evidences that some globular clusters are the stripped cores of larger dwarf galaxies previously massive enough to sustain multiple rounds of star formation. Its dense, concentrated core makes it appear stellar in small telescopes but resolves beautifully in larger instruments.

name: NGC6124
description: NGC 6124 is a bright, rich open cluster in Scorpius about 1,800 light-years away, containing around 100 member stars scattered across a wide field well matched to binocular or rich-field telescope views. Its estimated age of around 600 million years places it among moderately old open clusters, with several evolved red giants standing out against the brighter blue-white population. It lies in a dense Milky Way field that adds to the visual impression of richness.

name: NGC6541
description: NGC 6541 is a bright, rich globular cluster in Corona Australis about 22,800 light-years away, one of the more impressive globulars in the southern sky and often overlooked due to its southerly declination. It has a notably concentrated core and is estimated to be around 12 billion years old, placing it among the older Milky Way halo globulars. Under good skies it resolves into individual stars across its outer regions in a moderate telescope.

name: NGC3201
description: NGC 3201 is a loosely concentrated globular cluster in Vela about 16,300 light-years away, notable for its highly retrograde orbit, which carries it on a path counter to the rotation of the Milky Way disk. This unusual orbit strongly suggests it was captured from a dwarf galaxy that the Milky Way absorbed long ago. Studies of its stellar velocities have revealed evidence of a stellar-mass black hole in a binary system within the cluster, one of the first such detections in a globular.

name: NGC6352
description: NGC 6352 is a moderately bright globular cluster in Ara about 18,600 light-years away, characterized by a relatively low concentration and an unusual chemical composition suggesting it may have formed in the bulge of the Milky Way rather than the halo. Its loose, open structure makes individual stars resolvable across much of the cluster in moderate-aperture telescopes, and it lies in a rich southern Milky Way field. The cluster's age is estimated at around 12 billion years.

name: NGC6193
description: NGC 6193 is a bright, compact young open cluster in Ara about 4,300 light-years away, embedded within the emission nebula NGC 6188. The cluster's two most massive O-type stars are primarily responsible for ionizing the surrounding gas and sculpting the dramatic pillars and rims of NGC 6188 visible in narrowband images. At only around 3 million years old it is one of the youngest open clusters in the southern sky still intimately connected to its birth nebula.

name: NGC4945
description: NGC 4945 is a bright, nearly edge-on spiral galaxy in Centaurus about 13.1 million light-years away, a member of the Centaurus A/M83 Group. Its active galactic nucleus is one of the nearest and brightest Seyfert 2 galaxies, hidden behind a dense circumnuclear torus that blocks its optical light but is luminous in hard X-rays. Intense starburst activity in the nuclear disk drives a superwind of hot gas perpendicular to the disk, producing a spectacular gaseous outflow visible in X-ray and H-alpha images.

name: NGC5286
description: NGC 5286 is a rich, compact globular cluster in Centaurus about 35,900 light-years from Earth, notable for its large retrograde orbit and anomalous chemical abundances that have led some researchers to classify it as a possible former dwarf galaxy nucleus. Its high central concentration makes the core appear stellar in all but the largest amateur telescopes, while the outer regions resolve well in moderate apertures. It lies near the fourth-magnitude star M Centauri, making the two a striking visual pairing.

name: omi Vel Cluster
description: The Omicron Velorum Cluster (IC 2391) is one of the brightest and most prominent naked-eye open clusters in the southern sky, about 490 light-years away in Vela and containing roughly 30 members. At only around 50 million years old it is a young cluster still dominated by hot blue-white stars, with the fourth-magnitude star o Velorum as its brightest member. Its large apparent size of nearly 1 degree makes it a stunning binocular target under southern skies.

name: NGC1261
description: NGC 1261 is a compact, rich globular cluster in Horologium about 53,000 light-years from Earth, a member of the outer Milky Way halo. Studies of its radial velocity and orbit have shown it may be associated with the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger event, an ancient collision between the Milky Way and a massive dwarf galaxy that deposited many outer halo globulars. Its relatively small angular size and tight core concentration make it appear as a bright, unresolved knot in moderate telescopes.

name: NGC5823
description: NGC 5823 is a moderately rich open cluster in Circinus about 3,500 light-years away, containing roughly 100 stars of varying brightness. Its estimated age is around 600 million to one billion years, making it one of the older open clusters in this part of the Milky Way. The cluster is best viewed at low to moderate magnification in a southern telescope and lies in a region of patchy extinction from the Circinus molecular cloud complex.

name: S Nor Cluster
description: NGC 6087 is an open cluster in Norma about 3,500 light-years away, centered on the classical Cepheid variable star S Normae, one of the brightest Cepheids in the sky. The cluster is important because S Normae is a calibrator for the Cepheid period-luminosity relation, making NGC 6087 a benchmark for the extragalactic distance ladder. The cluster contains around 40 members and is estimated to be about 60 to 70 million years old.

name: NGC2867
description: NGC 2867 is a small, bright planetary nebula in Carina about 6,900 light-years away, displaying a vivid blue-green disk at moderate magnification. Its compact, nearly circular appearance and high surface brightness make it one of the most easily identified southern planetary nebulae in a telescope. A hot central white dwarf powers the nebula's ionization, and its nearly round shape suggests a symmetric outflow from the central star.

name: NGC6025
description: NGC 6025 is a bright, moderately rich open cluster in Triangulum Australe about 2,700 light-years away, containing around 60 member stars. It is one of the finest open clusters in the southern Milky Way accessible to binoculars, with a prominent central concentration of blue-white stars and a handful of slightly evolved yellowish members. Its estimated age of around 75 to 100 million years places it in the younger bracket of open clusters in this region of the galaxy.

name: NGC2516
description: NGC 2516 is a large, rich open cluster in Carina about 1,300 light-years away, containing around 300 confirmed members and comparable in appearance to the Pleiades but slightly farther and richer. Its estimated age of around 150 million years is notable for producing early studies comparing stellar rotation rates in the cluster to those in the Hyades and Pleiades to calibrate gyrochronology. A brilliant central red giant contrasts strikingly with the surrounding blue-white members.

name: Pearl Cluster
description: The Pearl Cluster (NGC 3766) is a bright, rich young open cluster in Centaurus about 6,900 light-years away, known for the sparkling visual impression its densely packed blue-white stars give at low magnification. With an estimated age of only about 14 million years it is a very young cluster, and a 2013 study of its rapid rotators discovered a new class of periodic variable stars not predicted by standard stellar models. The cluster contains over 100 confirmed members and is a showpiece of the southern Milky Way.

name: Coalsack Cluster
description: NGC 4609 is a compact open cluster in Crux about 5,700 light-years away, lying directly adjacent to the Coalsack dark nebula (C99) in the sky. It contains around 40 stars in a moderately concentrated arrangement and is estimated to be around 45 million years old. The visual juxtaposition of this glittering cluster against the jet-black backdrop of the Coalsack makes it a striking wide-field pairing in photographs and binocular views.

name: C99
description: The Coalsack is the most prominent dark nebula in the sky, a massive molecular cloud in Crux about 600 light-years away that appears as a strikingly dark, roughly oval void against the dense Milky Way star fields of the Southern Cross region. Spanning about 7 by 5 degrees on the sky, it is readily visible to the naked eye as one of the darkest patches in the entire Milky Way. Indigenous Australian peoples have long included the Coalsack in their astronomical traditions as part of the Emu in the Sky, a constellation defined by dark nebulae rather than stars.

name: lam Cen Nebula
description: IC 2944 is an active HII region and open cluster complex in Centaurus about 6,500 light-years away, surrounding the young star cluster IC 2948 whose O-type members ionize the surrounding gas. It is famous for its population of Bok globules, dark molecular condensations nicknamed Thackeray's Globules that are among the largest and most visually striking such objects known. Long-exposure narrowband images show an intricate landscape of glowing hydrogen gas, dark columns, and evaporating protostellar cocoons.

name: NGC6744
description: NGC 6744 is a large, loosely wound barred spiral galaxy in Pavo about 30 million light-years away, considered one of the closest analogs to the Milky Way in the local universe in terms of size, mass, and overall morphology. Its face-on orientation reveals sweeping spiral arms rich in star-forming regions and a prominent central bar, along with a nearby irregular companion NGC 6744A reminiscent of the Large Magellanic Cloud. Its low surface brightness and great apparent size of roughly 20 arcminutes make it a challenging visual target but a rewarding photographic one.

name: NGC362
description: NGC 362 is a bright, compact globular cluster in Tucana about 27,700 light-years away, appearing in the same wide-field view as the Small Magellanic Cloud and the globular 47 Tucanae (C106). It is unusually metal-rich for such a large, massive cluster, and its stellar population analysis reveals evidence of multiple stellar generations. Its high central concentration makes it difficult to resolve in small telescopes but a beautiful tight ball of stars in larger instruments.

name: NGC4833
description: NGC 4833 is a loosely concentrated globular cluster in Musca about 21,200 light-years away, notably reddened by foreground interstellar dust that limits its apparent brightness compared to its true luminosity. It orbits on a retrograde path close to the Galactic plane, where it experiences strong tidal forces, and its outer regions are less populated than expected, possibly due to ongoing tidal stripping. Its loose concentration class makes individual stars resolvable in moderate-aperture telescopes.

name: NGC6101
description: NGC 6101 is a loosely concentrated globular cluster in Apus about 49,500 light-years from Earth, one of the more remote Milky Way halo globulars. Studies have proposed it may be associated with the Gaia-Enceladus accretion event based on its retrograde orbit and chemical abundances. Its low central concentration and distant location make it a faint, poorly resolved object in moderate apertures, appearing as a granular haze rather than a resolved stellar system.

name: NGC4372
description: NGC 4372 is a large, loosely concentrated globular cluster in Musca about 19,000 light-years away, heavily reddened by foreground interstellar dust. Its enormous apparent angular diameter of around 20 arcminutes makes it one of the largest apparent globulars in the sky, but the combined effect of reddening and its low concentration means it is poorly detected in small instruments and best appreciated in wide-field photographs. It is noticeably metal-poor compared with most Milky Way globulars, placing it among the oldest and most primordial stellar systems known.

name: NGC3195
description: NGC 3195 is a bright planetary nebula in Chamaeleon about 6,700 light-years away, one of the most southerly planetary nebulae observable from most populated latitudes. Its nearly circular disk is compact but readily visible in moderate-aperture telescopes under clear southern skies, appearing as a pale blue-gray disk at high magnification. It is one of the farthest-south objects in the Caldwell catalog and inaccessible to most northern hemisphere observers even at the most southern continental observing sites.

name: NGC157
description: NGC 157 is an intermediate spiral galaxy in the constellation of Cetus, positioned about 4° east of the star Iota Ceti. This galaxy can be viewed from suburban skies using a moderate-sized telescope.

name: NGC2527
description: NGC 2527 is an open cluster in the constellation Puppis. It was discovered by William Herschel on December 9, 1784.

name: NGC2782
description: NGC 2782 is a peculiar spiral galaxy that formed after a galaxy merger in the constellation Lynx. The galaxy lies 75 million light years away from Earth, which means, given its apparent dimensions, that NGC 2782 is approximately 100,000 light years across.

name: NGC3226
description: NGC 3226 is a dwarf elliptical galaxy that is interacting with the spiral galaxy NGC 3227. They were both discovered by German-British astronomer William Herschel on 15 February 1784.

name: NGC3395
description: NGC 3395 is a peculiar spiral galaxy in the constellation Leo Minor. The galaxy lies about 55 million light years away from Earth, which means, given its apparent dimensions, that NGC 3395 is approximately 35,000 light years across.

name: NGC3504
description: NGC 3504 is a barred spiral galaxy in the constellation Leo Minor. It has a Hubble distance corresponding to 88 million light-years and was discovered by William Herschel in 1785.

name: NGC3619
description: NGC 3619 is an unbarred lenticular galaxy located in the constellation Ursa Major. It was discovered by the astronomer William Herschel on March 18, 1790.

name: NGC4346
description: NGC 4346 is a lenticular galaxy located in the constellation Canes Venatici about 50 million light-years away. It was discovered on April 1, 1788 by the astronomer William Herschel.

name: NGC4536
description: NGC 4536 is an intermediate spiral galaxy in the constellation Virgo. It was discovered by German-British astronomer William Herschel on 24 January 1784.

name: NGC5273
description: NGC 5273 is a lenticular galaxy located 54 million light-years away in the northern constellation of Canes Venatici. This galaxy was discovered by William Herschel on May 1, 1785. It is positioned 1+1⁄4° to the southeast of the star 25 Canum Venaticorum.

name: NGC5676
description: NGC 5676 is an unbarred spiral galaxy in the constellation Boötes.

name: NGC6144
description: NGC 6144 is a globular cluster in the constellation Scorpius, located almost exactly 1° away from its brighter counterpart globular cluster Messier 4. It is relatively close to and is partially obscured by the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex.

name: NGC6217
description: NGC 6217 is a barred spiral galaxy located some 67 million light years away, in the constellation Ursa Minor. The galaxy is inclined by an angle of 33° to the line of sight along a position angle of 162°.

name: NGC6520
description: NGC 6520 is an open cluster of stars in the southern constellation of Sagittarius, about 4° to the east of the Galactic Center. Just to the west of this cluster is the dark nebula Barnard 86, dubbed the Ink Spot.

name: NGC6624
description: NGC 6624 is a globular cluster in the constellation Sagittarius. It was discovered on 24 June 1784 by the astronomer William Herschel.

name: NGC6755
description: NGC 6755 is an open cluster of stars in the equatorial constellation of Aquila, positioned about 3° to the east of the star Delta Aquilae. It was discovered by the Anglo-German astronomer William Herschel on July 30, 1785 and is located at a distance of 8,060 light years from the Sun.

name: NGC6756
description: NGC 6756 is a small open star cluster in the constellation Aquila, close to NGC 6755.

name: NGC7790
description: NGC 7790 is a young open cluster of stars located some 10,800 light years away from Earth in the northern constellation of Cassiopeia. NGC 7790 has a Trumpler class rating of II2m and the estimated age is 60–80 million years.

name: NGC2185
description: NGC 2185 is a nebula in the constellation Monoceros, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 12.9, spanning about 2 arcminutes, it is a faint target best suited to larger telescopes or long-exposure imaging.

name: NGC3912
description: NGC 3912 is a galaxy in the constellation Leo, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 13.16, spanning about 2 arcminutes, it is a faint target best suited to larger telescopes or long-exposure imaging.

name: NGC4085
description: NGC 4085 is a galaxy in the constellation Ursa Major, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 12.37, spanning about 2 arcminutes, it is a faint target best suited to larger telescopes or long-exposure imaging.

name: NGC4143
description: NGC 4143 is a galaxy in the constellation Canes Venatici, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 12.08, spanning about 3 arcminutes, it is a faint target best suited to larger telescopes or long-exposure imaging.

name: NGC6583
description: NGC 6583 is an open cluster in the constellation Sagittarius, part of the Herschel 400 observing list. At magnitude 10, spanning about 4 arcminutes, it is a modest target for amateur telescopes.

name: IC1470
description: IC 1470 is a nebula in Cepheus. It was first discovered by Rudolf Ferdinand Spitaler on 20 March, 1892. The following night it was independently discovered by Carl Frederick Pechüle and Edward Emerson Barnard.

name: SH2-2
description: Sh 2-2, also known as Sharpless 2, is an emission nebula in the constellation of Scorpius. It appears as a mid-range brightness making it difficult to view. It is believed to currently host an X-ray binary star that originated and was ejected from the Scorpius OB1 association. Amateur astronomers can usually see it with a wide field telescope and a hydrogen-alpha filter.

name: Forgotten Nebula
description: Sh 2-34, also known as the Forgotten Nebula is a nebula in Sagittarius. It is a star-forming region and contains multiple filamentary structures. Most of the nebula is composed of hydrogen and sulfur, with a region of oxygen.

name: IC1283
description: Sh 2-37, also known by the designation IC 1284, or the common name Twiddlebug Nebula, is an emission nebula in the constellation Sagittarius. It is located is the direction of ionizing star cluster Dias 5. It also contains the radio source W 34.

name: SH2-64
description: Westerhout 40 or W40 is a star-forming region in the Milky Way located in the constellation Serpens. In this region, interstellar gas forming a diffuse nebula surrounds a cluster of several hundred new-born stars. The distance to W40 is 436 ± 9 pc, making it one of the closest sites of formation of high-mass O-type and B-type stars. The ionizing radiation from the massive OB stars has created an H II region, which has an hour-glass morphology.

name: SNR G65.3+5.7
description: SNR G65.3+5.7, also known as the Little Veil Nebula, is a supernova remnant in Cygnus. It is made up of multiple Sharpless Objects. Sh 2-92, Sh 2-94, and Sh 2-96.

name: SH2-103
description: The Cygnus Loop is a large supernova remnant (SNR) in the constellation Cygnus, an emission nebula measuring nearly 3° across. Some arcs of the loop, known collectively as the Veil Nebula or Cirrus Nebula, emit in the visible electromagnetic range. Radio, infrared, and X-ray images reveal the complete loop.

name: Flying Dragon Nebula
description: Sh 2-113 also known as the Flying Dragon Nebula or LBN 333, is a nebula that resembles a supernova remnant (SNR) but with no evidence to support it being an SNR. Sh 2-113 is located in the northern hemisphere constellation of Cygnus south of the star Deneb. Nearby are the planetary nebulae K 2-81, Kn 26 and LBN 346.

name: Elephant's Trunk Nebula
description: The Elephant's Trunk Nebula is a concentration of interstellar gas and dust within the much larger ionized gas region IC 1396 located in the constellation Cepheus about 2,400 light years away from Earth. The nebula is a dark, dense globule that gets its name from its appearance at visible light wavelengths, where there is a dark patch with a bright, sinuous rim. The bright rim is the surface of the dense cloud that is being illuminated and ionized by a very bright, massive multiple star that is just to the east of the Elephant's Trunk Nebula. The entire IC 1396 region is ionized by the massive star, except for dense globules that can protect themselves from the star's harsh ultraviolet rays.

name: Little Rosette Nebula
description: Sharpless 2-170, also known by the common name the Little Rosette Nebula is an emission nebula in the constellation Cassiopeia.

name: Simeis 22
description: Simeis 22, also known as the Firefox Nebula, is a planetary nebula in Cassiopeia. It was discovered in the early 1950s by Grigory Shajn and Vera Gaze. It was independently discovered by Stewart Sharpless. It was first thought to be a supernova remnant, and was then thought to be a planetary nebula.

name: Heart Nebula
description:
The Heart Nebula is an emission nebula, 7,500 light-years (2,300 pc) away from Earth and located in the Perseus Arm of the Galaxy in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was discovered by William Herschel on 3 November 1787. In 1958, it was identified as a radio source by Gart Westerhout and is therefore also referred to as Westerhout 4 .
It displays glowing ionized hydrogen gas and darker dust lanes.

name: Maffei 1
description: Maffei 1 is a massive elliptical galaxy near the constellation borders between Perseus and Cassiopeia, located 9.8 million light years away. Once believed to be a member of the Local Group of galaxies, it is now known to belong to a separate group, the IC 342/Maffei Group. It was named after Paolo Maffei, who discovered it and the neighboring Maffei 2 in 1967 via their infrared emissions.

name: Maffei 2
description: Maffei 2 is an intermediate spiral galaxy about 10 million light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia. Maffei 2 and Maffei 1 were both discovered by Paolo Maffei in 1968 from their infrared emission. Maffei 2 lies in the Zone of Avoidance and is about 99.5% obscured by the Milky Way's foreground dust clouds, and as a result is barely detectable at optical wavelengths. It had been suggested soon after its discovery that Maffei 2 may be a member of the Local Group, but it is now thought to be a member of another nearby group, the IC 342/Maffei Group, the galaxy group that is the closest to the Local Group.

name: Rosette Nebula
description: The Rosette Nebula is an H II region located near one end of a giant molecular cloud in the Monoceros region of the Milky Way Galaxy. The open cluster NGC 2244 is closely associated with the nebulosity, the stars of the cluster having been formed from the nebula's matter.

name: NGC1973
description: Sh 2-279 is an HII region and bright nebulae that includes a reflection nebula located in the constellation Orion. Alternatively, it is designated S279 or Sharpless 279. This feature is the northernmost part of the asterism known as Orion's Sword, lying 0.6° north of the Orion Nebula. The reflection nebula embedded in Sh 2-279 is popularly known as the Running Man Nebula.

name: Abell 31
description: Abell 31 is an ancient planetary nebula in the constellation of Cancer. It is estimated to be about 2,000 light years away. The central white dwarf has a spectral type of DAO.

name: Seagull Nebula
description: IC 2177 is a region of nebulosity that lies along the border between the constellations Monoceros and Canis Major. It is a roughly circular H II region centered on the Be star HD 53367. This nebula was discovered by Welsh amateur astronomer Isaac Roberts and was described by him as "pretty bright, extremely large, irregularly round, very diffuse."

name: SH2-297
description:
Sh 2-297 is an emission nebula in the constellation Canis Major.
The region was catalogued in 1959 in the extended seconded edition of the Sharpless catalogue. This area is part of the Canis Major OB1 Association, and is a very active area of new star formation.

name: Abell 35
description: Abell 35, also known as Sh 2-313, is a nebula located in the constellation of Hydra, at a distance of 400 light years.
